guides.title: Search and Rescue Planning Cycle
guides.summary: How a land search for a missing person is actually planned and run: taking the first report, fixing the last known point, using lost person behavior statistics, building and segmenting a search area, probability of area and detection, choosing tactics, briefing and debriefing teams, running operational periods, managing clues, and deciding when to scale back.

sections.heading: Why a Search Is an Emergency — the Planning Cycle at a Glance
sections.body:
The founding principle of modern land search is a sentence drilled into every search manager: a search is an emergency. It feels counterintuitive, because a missing person report arrives without sirens — no smoke, no wreckage, just an absence. But the mathematics of survival and of search both punish delay. A mobile, uninjured subject moves farther every hour, and the area that must be examined grows roughly with the square of the distance they could have traveled; a subject who is injured, hypothermic, very young or very old is meanwhile losing physiological reserve. Studies of search incidents repeatedly show that survival probability falls steeply after the first twenty-four to seventy-two hours, with the exact curve depending on weather, age and condition. Every hour spent waiting to see if they turn up is an hour donated to the problem.

Because of that urgency, search management is organized as a cycle rather than a single plan. The cycle runs continuously: gather information, form a picture of what probably happened, define where the subject could be, decide where to look first and with what, send teams, get their results back, and feed everything learned — including the places the subject was not found — into the next turn of the wheel. The cycle repeats until the subject is found or a deliberate, documented decision is made to change the objective. Each pass through the loop should make the picture sharper, because negative information is still information: an empty trail eliminates possibilities and shifts probability elsewhere.

The cycle has recognizable stages that the rest of this guide walks through in order. First notice is the moment the emergency system learns someone is missing, and the initial report sets everything else in motion. Investigation builds the subject profile — who this person is, what they were doing, and what they are likely to do now. The planning side then establishes the last known point, constructs a search area, divides it into workable segments, and assigns probabilities. The operations side turns that into assignments: hasty teams on trails, grid teams in segments, dogs, trackers, aircraft, drones. Briefing sends teams out knowing what to look for; debriefing extracts everything they saw and how well they covered their ground. The planning section digests debriefs and re-plans, and the next operational period begins.

Two mindsets keep the cycle honest. The first is that the search is for clues, not just for the subject: one person is a single object in a huge landscape, but a walking person sheds a trail of evidence — footprints, dropped items, scent, broken vegetation, witnesses — and any one clue can collapse the search area dramatically. The second is humility before uncertainty: the plan is a set of bets, stated as probabilities, and the cycle exists precisely so the bets get revised as evidence arrives rather than defended out of pride. Well-run searches are distinguishable less by luck than by how fast and honestly they update.

Finally, the cycle sits inside a formal management structure, usually the Incident Command System, so that as a search grows from three people at a trailhead to hundreds with aircraft, the planning loop keeps turning at every scale without anyone losing track of who decided what, and why.

sections.heading: First Notice — Taking the Initial Report
sections.body:
Every search begins with a report, and the quality of that first conversation shapes the whole incident. First notice usually arrives by telephone — a spouse whose partner is overdue from a hike, a campground host, a hunting companion — or in person at a trailhead or police station. The person taking that call has two jobs at once: to gather specific, checkable facts, and to gauge urgency, because the response to an overdue teenager with a phone differs from the response to a missing three-year-old near a river at dusk.

The core facts follow the old journalism questions. Who is missing: name, age, sex, physical description, clothing and footwear in detail — sole pattern matters enormously to trackers — plus medical conditions, medications and how long the person can miss them, fitness, experience, and mental state. What were they doing: day hike, hunting, berry picking, driving between towns, walking away from a care facility. When and where were they last seen, and by whom, stated precisely rather than vaguely — at the trail junction at about 14:30, not this afternoon somewhere up there. What equipment do they carry: food, water, shelter, light, map, phone. What has already been done: many families search for hours before calling, and knowing which roads and trails they already drove or walked, and that they shouted and honked, changes both urgency and planning.

Good report-takers use structured forms — commonly called a lost person questionnaire or missing person report — precisely because stress makes people forget to ask the obvious. The form prompts for the reporting party's own details and relationship to the subject, for vehicle descriptions and plate numbers, for the subject's phone number and carrier, for a recent photograph, and for the names of anyone else who might know the subject's plans. It also prompts for the uncomfortable questions that must be asked early and tactfully: recent arguments, depression or suicidal statements, alcohol and drugs, domestic trouble, dementia diagnoses, and whether the person has gone missing before and where they were found. Investigators return to these because a significant fraction of missing adults are voluntarily missing or despondent, and those cases concentrate in different places than lost hikers.

Urgency is then assessed deliberately rather than by gut alone. Widely taught relative-urgency worksheets score the subject's age, medical condition, the weather now and coming, the terrain and hazards, the subject's equipment and experience, and the number of subjects — a lone subject is generally judged more urgent than a pair, since two people can share warmth and judgment. High urgency triggers immediate response with whatever resources are nearest; lower urgency may justify investigation first. Crucially, urgency is re-scored as facts change: a routine overdue-hiker call becomes urgent when the forecast turns or when the phone company reports the phone dead since noon.

Two actions belong to first notice even before planning starts. First, protect the point last seen and the subject's vehicle or room from trampling and disturbance — they are clue-rich scenes, and scent articles for dog teams should be secured early in a paper bag, handled as little as possible. Second, start a written log. From the first call onward, every fact, decision, time and name goes on paper or into the incident software, because searches are legally scrutinized events and because the planning cycle runs on recorded, time-stamped information rather than memory.

sections.heading: The Last Known Point, the Point Last Seen and the Initial Planning Point
sections.body:
Search planning is geometry anchored to a point, so the first planning task is deciding exactly which point. The vocabulary matters. The point last seen, abbreviated PLS, is where a witness actually saw the subject — a companion watched him walk over the ridge at the saddle. The last known point, LKP, is the most recent location the subject can be placed by physical evidence rather than eyewitness memory: the car at the trailhead, a signature in a summit register, a purchase receipt, a cell phone ping, a footprint matching the subject's boot. A search may begin with a PLS and then acquire better LKPs as investigation proceeds; a found clue — a dropped glove identified by the family — becomes the new LKP and can move the center of the whole search.

From these, planners designate the initial planning point, the IPP: the anchor from which the search area is constructed and from which distances in the lost person behavior statistics are measured. The IPP is normally the best available LKP or PLS at the time planning starts. Choosing it deserves real thought, because everything downstream — rings, probability zones, segment priorities — inherits its errors. A car at a trailhead is a strong IPP for a hiker; for a despondent subject who left home on foot, the residence may serve; for a driver, the vehicle wherever it is found typically resets the entire problem around it.

Verification is the discipline that keeps the anchor honest. Eyewitness reports are notoriously soft: people confuse days, misjudge times, and misidentify strangers as the subject. Good practice is to grade every sighting by source reliability and corroboration, to re-interview key witnesses separately, and to physically confirm what can be confirmed — walk to the claimed junction, find the register, pull the receipt, request phone records through proper channels. Cell phone data deserves its own mention: an exact GPS fix from a modern emergency location service can nearly solve a search, while a mere association with a tower only draws a large arc of possibility, and planners must understand the difference before redrawing the map around a ping.

Once fixed, the IPP and its surroundings are treated with forensic respect. The immediate area — commonly the first hundred meters or so — is searched carefully and early for the direction-of-travel evidence that pays the biggest dividends: footprints leaving the trailhead, which fork of the trail the tread follows, fence crossings, dropped items. Trackers call establishing this the step-by-step or sign-cutting phase, and a confirmed direction of travel can cut the search area in half at a stroke. This is also why vehicles are not casually opened and areas not flooded with untasked volunteers: every well-meaning boot erases the highest-value square meters of the entire incident.

Finally, planners record the time attached to the IPP as carefully as the place, because the search area is a function of both. A subject last seen at 09:00 yesterday defines a very different problem from the same point at 21:00 last night, and the elapsed-time clock — hours the subject has had to move, and hours of exposure they have endured — starts from that timestamp, not from when the search was requested.

sections.heading: Investigation — Building the Subject Profile
sections.body:
While maps are being drawn, a parallel and equally important effort is pure investigation, because a search is as much a missing person case as a wilderness exercise. The goal is a subject profile rich enough to predict behavior: not just what the subject looks like, but how they think, what they fear, what they would do when tired, and where they may have intended to go. Search managers commonly assign specific personnel to investigation for the life of the incident, and on many searches the case is broken not by a field team but by a phone call.

The profile starts with the extended lost person questionnaire and radiates outward through interviews. Family and companions are interviewed separately, both because memories contaminate each other and because sensitive matters — depression, addiction, marital trouble, debts, a new relationship — surface more honestly one-on-one. Friends, coworkers, hiking partners and social media often know plans the family does not: an intended route posted online, a peak-bagging list, a favorite fishing hole, a person they meant to meet. Investigators check the subject's home or room, with consent or warrant as required, for missing gear that reveals intent — absent boots and daypack tell a different story from absent car keys and passport — and for notes, maps with marked routes, and browser history about destinations.

Records extend the interviews. Phone activity, banking transactions, transit cards and toll records can place a subject in time and space and are pursued through law enforcement channels. Trail registers, permit systems, hut logbooks and parking records place them in the landscape. Previous incidents matter greatly: people who have been lost before are often found in the same kinds of places, and facilities caring for people with dementia frequently keep records of prior wandering routes, which are among the best predictors available.

A specific investigative duty is testing the assumption that the subject is missing in the search area at all. The scenario analysis should always carry a line item variously called rest of world or bastard search — the possibility that the subject left the area, is at a friend's house, took a bus home, or was never there. Hospitals, jails, transit police, taxi companies and the subject's own residence are checked and rechecked; embarrassing numbers of major searches have ended with the subject found asleep at home or drinking in a nearby town. Checking the mundane possibilities early is not a distraction from the field effort; it protects it, because every hour of grid searching is wasted if the premise is wrong.

Investigation also drives scenario building, the explicit list of stories that could explain the disappearance: took a wrong turn at the junction and descended the wrong drainage; injured on the scramble section; despondent and seeking solitude near water; picked up by a friend. Each scenario implies places and clue types, and planners keep the list alive on a wall where new information can promote, demote or kill scenarios visibly. The discipline of writing scenarios down guards against the classic failure of search management — locking onto one story early and unconsciously filtering all later evidence through it. The investigation section's job, permanently, is to keep asking what else could be true and what one phone call would test it.

sections.heading: Lost Person Behavior — What the Statistics Say
sections.body:
The single most useful planning tool after the map is the accumulated statistical behavior of previously lost people. Lost people are not random particles; they are running predictable software — human perception, fear, energy budgets and terrain response — and decades of case data show strong regularities by subject category. The landmark modern compilation is Robert Koester's book Lost Person Behavior, published in 2008 and built on the International Search and Rescue Incident Database, ISRID, which by later editions aggregated well over a hundred thousand incidents from multiple countries. Search planners use these statistics not as prophecy but as prior probabilities: where people like this, in terrain like this, have historically ended up.

The data are organized by subject category because behavior differs sharply. Hikers dominate wilderness caseloads and tend to follow travel aids — trails, roads, drainages — and to be found at moderate distances from the IPP. Hunters travel farther off-trail, focused on game rather than navigation, and are often found in surprisingly rough spots. Children split by age band: very young children, roughly one to three, have no navigation concept, tend to seek shelter and are often found close, sometimes hidden and unresponsive to shouting; children four to six travel farther, may deliberately hide from strangers or from expected punishment; older children behave increasingly like adults. People with dementia are a critical special category: they typically travel in relatively straight lines until stopped by an obstacle, do not call out, do not respond to their name, and are frequently found within sight of a road or in dense brush a short distance from a route — and their survival window is short, which raises urgency automatically. Despondent subjects are usually found near the interface between civilization and seclusion — a viewpoint, the edge of a park — and typically within a modest distance of the point last seen. Anglers are found near water; climbers on or beneath their route; mushroom and berry pickers, eyes down, are among the most-lost of all recreational categories.

The headline numbers planners actually use are distance-from-IPP distributions, quoted as quartiles: for each category and terrain type, the distance rings within which twenty-five, fifty, seventy-five and ninety-five percent of subjects were found. For temperate-zone hikers, for example, published tables put the median find distance on the order of two kilometers, with ninety-five percent inside roughly ten; for small children the distances are much shorter. Rings drawn at those radii around the IPP become an instant, defensible first-cut probability map. Alongside distances, the tables report dispersion angle from the direction of travel, elevation change — lost subjects generally descend more often than climb — mobility duration, and find location type: how often the category is found on a linear feature, in structures, in brush, or by water. Survivability tables complete the picture, relating hours missing, weather and age to the probability of survival, which informs both urgency and, later, suspension decisions.

Using the statistics well means respecting their limits. They are aggregates over many landscapes; a cliff band or a swollen river in the actual search area overrides any table. They describe find locations, which are biased toward where people searched. And every individual can be an outlier. The proper use is Bayesian in spirit: statistics set the initial bets, the investigation adjusts them to this particular human being, and field evidence then revises everything — which is exactly the planning cycle turning.

sections.heading: Reflex Tasks — Containment and the Hasty Search
sections.body:
Before the deliberate planning machinery produces its first full plan, experienced managers launch a set of reflex tasks — immediate actions so consistently valuable that they are ordered on nearly every search, in parallel with planning rather than after it. They exploit the early hours, when the subject is closest, most alive and most mobile, and when clues are freshest.

The first reflex is containment: stopping the search area from growing. A moving subject expands the problem hour by hour, so planners establish a perimeter of blocks and lookouts. Trail junctions and road crossings on the likely routes are posted or patrolled; trailheads get personnel who log everyone leaving; prominent points may get spotters with binoculars. Where staffing is thin, teams set track traps — swept or raked patches of ground across trails and probable corridors that will record a footprint of anyone passing — and check them on a schedule, which converts a dirt road into an unattended sensor line. Some operations add attraction to containment: vehicle lights and sirens at road heads at night, whistle or horn signals on a published pattern, and in suitable cases a fixed light or fire visible across a basin, so that a mobile, responsive subject can find the searchers. Attraction has solved searches outright, and it costs almost nothing; its main caution is coordination, so that signals are consistent and any response — three whistle blasts, a light flashed back — is recognized and reported.

The second reflex is the hasty search, sometimes formalized as Type I search. Small, fast, self-sufficient teams of two or three — often the most experienced field people available — immediately travel the high-probability linear features and spots: the trail the subject planned, its junctions and drainages, streambeds, ridgelines, huts, viewpoints, water sources, and known hazards such as cliff bases and river crossings. Hasty teams move quickly, calling the subject's name, stopping to listen on a rhythm, checking the mud of every junction for tread, and marking or photographing anything of interest without trampling it. They are simultaneously searching, clue-hunting and reconnoitering: their reports about terrain, snow line, water levels and travel times feed directly into the segmenting and tasking that planning is doing back at base. Dog teams and trackers, if available early, are classic hasty resources — a trailing dog started promptly from the PLS on a clean scent article, before the area is contaminated, has the best chance it will ever have.

The third reflex is investigation of the immediate scene, already described: protecting and working the IPP for direction of travel, and securing the vehicle. A fourth, easily forgotten, is checking the obvious quickly — the subject's home, the parking lots, the visitor center, the nearest bar — because the cheapest find is the embarrassing one.

Reflex tasking illustrates a principle that runs through the whole cycle: planning and acting are simultaneous, not sequential. A search that waits to act until the plan is perfect wastes the golden hours; a search that acts without ever planning dissolves into motion without coverage. The reflex tasks are the standing bridge between the two — pre-decided actions of high expected value, launched while the map work catches up. When the first operational period is formally planned, the hasty results are already in hand: trails cleared or bearing tread, containment established, dogs committed, and often the first real clue on the board.

sections.heading: Building the Search Area — Theoretical, Statistical and Deductive Methods
sections.body:
With an anchor point fixed and a profile forming, planners must draw the line that bounds the problem: the search area, the region within which the subject is assumed to be. Drawing it too small risks excluding the subject entirely; drawing it too big dilutes effort below usefulness. Standard doctrine attacks the boundary from several independent directions and then overlays the results, on the sound logic that methods with different weaknesses fail in different places.

The theoretical method asks the physics question: how far could this subject possibly have traveled since the IPP time? Multiply elapsed time by a defensible travel rate for this person in this terrain — a fit hiker on trails might manage four or five kilometers per hour for some hours; a frail elderly walker off-trail, a small fraction of that — and draw the resulting circle. The honest version subtracts rest and darkness and respects terrain, producing not a neat circle but a travel-time contour, and modern planning software computes exactly that from slope and land cover. The theoretical area is almost always enormous, and that is its point: it is the outer fence, the statement of the worst case, and anything outside it can be excluded on physical grounds alone.

The statistical method applies the lost person behavior tables: rings at the twenty-five, fifty, seventy-five and ninety-five percent find distances for the subject's category and terrain. This yields a much smaller, probability-weighted core. Its weakness is the aggregate nature of the data — it knows nothing about this landscape's particular funnels and barriers — which is precisely what the next method supplies.

The deductive or subjective method is local reasoning on the actual map with the actual scenario list. Terrain analysis identifies barriers that stop or deflect travel — cliff bands, canyons, rivers, dense blowdown, fenced highways — and travel aids that channel it: trails, roads, powerline cuts, open ridges, drainages. Human factors join in: lost people tend to go downhill, to follow the path of least resistance, to be drawn toward lights and sounds at night, and to hit a linear feature and turn along it. Each scenario from the investigation is traced onto the map as the routes and destinations it implies — if he missed the junction in fog, he descended this drainage toward that road — and the union of scenario traces, clipped by barriers, marks the deductively likely region. Local knowledge is gold here: rangers, hunters and old-timers know where previous subjects were found, where trails braid confusingly, which slopes cliff out, and where everyone ends up when they lose this particular path.

The fourth input, often decisive, is clues and technology: a confirmed footprint, a phone ping arc, a witness sighting graded reliable — each redraws the area around itself, sometimes abandoning the original IPP entirely.

The final search area is the reconciliation of all of these, typically the statistical core expanded and reshaped by deduction, bounded by the theoretical fence, and annotated with the containment perimeter already established. Two bookkeeping rules finish the job. First, the boundary is a working assumption, recorded with its reasoning, and revisited every planning cycle — subjects are found outside the ninety-five percent ring five percent of the time, by definition. Second, the world outside the boundary is never probability zero: the rest-of-world scenario stays on the board, funded by investigation rather than boot leather, until the subject is found somewhere.

sections.heading: Probability of Area — Dividing Belief Across the Map
sections.body:
Once the search area exists, planners must express how strongly they believe in each part of it, because effort should follow belief. The formal quantity is probability of area, POA — for each defined region, the probability that the subject is in it. Assigning POA converts hunches into numbers that can be argued about, documented, and updated, which is the entire administrative point: numbers force explicitness, and explicitness exposes weak reasoning before it wastes a day of searching.

The standard technique for initial POA is structured consensus, and the classic version is the Mattson method, introduced by Robert Mattson in the 1970s. The search area is divided into named regions — often the scenario regions or early segments — and each member of a small planning group independently and privately distributes one hundred percentage points across those regions, always including a rest-of-world entry for the possibility that the subject is outside the area altogether. Independence is the crucial feature: private assignment before discussion prevents the loudest or most senior voice from anchoring everyone else, which is a well-documented group failure. The individual allocations are then averaged region by region to produce the working POA table. Variants refine the mechanics: the proportional method has planners score each region on an open scale, say one to ten, with the scores normalized to percentages afterward, which people often find more natural than forcing a hundred-point budget; the O'Connor approach similarly separates relative weighting from normalization. Whichever arithmetic is used, disagreement among planners is itself data — a region scored five percent by one planner and thirty by another signals an unshared assumption that should be argued out loud, and the argument is usually worth more than the average.

Several disciplines keep POA meaningful. The regions must be exhaustive and non-overlapping, so the numbers can legitimately sum to one hundred. The basis of each allocation should be recorded in a sentence — high because the drainage catches everyone who misses the junction — so that when facts change, the affected allocations can be found and revised rather than the whole table being re-guessed. Rest of world must be taken seriously, not parked at a token one percent; historical experience with subjects found far outside search areas, or never in them, justifies honest double-digit values early in many incidents, declining as investigation eliminates the outside explanations.

POA is a living quantity, updated in two ways. Clues update it upward: a verified footprint in a region concentrates probability there, and a strong enough clue can justify re-running the consensus entirely around a new picture. Unsuccessful search updates it downward, mechanically: when a region is searched with some probability of detection and the subject is not found, Bayesian arithmetic shifts probability out of that region into the unsearched ones — the formal machinery for the intuition that the more thoroughly we have looked here, the more likely they are elsewhere. The next section builds the detection half of that arithmetic.

A final caution keeps the numbers in their place. POA quantifies belief given current information; it does not manufacture knowledge. A beautifully maintained probability table built on a wrong assumption — the wrong trailhead, a misremembered sighting — is precise nonsense. That is why the cycle pairs the mathematics with relentless investigation, and why every planning meeting should begin by asking what, since the last meeting, would change the table if true.

sections.heading: Segmenting the Map — Making the Area Searchable
sections.body:
Probability regions answer where we believe; segments answer where a team can actually be sent. Segmenting divides the search area into pieces sized and bounded so that one resource can search one segment in one work session, and so that everyone can agree afterward exactly what ground was and was not covered. It is unglamorous cartographic work, and it is where many searches are quietly won or lost, because coverage claims are only as trustworthy as the boundaries they refer to.

Good segments follow recognizable boundaries on the ground, not just lines on a map: trails, streams, ridgelines, roads, fence lines, the edge of a burn. A field team must be able to stand in the landscape and know which side of the boundary it is on without a debate; boundaries that exist only as grid lines produce overlaps and gaps that nobody detects until the debrief map shows two teams claiming the same slope while the gully between them was never entered. Where nature provides no feature, searches manufacture boundaries with flagging tape or rely on GPS corridors, but natural features are always preferred because they are unambiguous in fog, at night and in thick timber.

Size is dictated by search speed, not by neatness. A common rule of thumb sizes a segment so a ground team can cover it to a reasonable thoroughness in roughly four to six hours — long enough to be efficient, short enough that the team returns within the operational period with results while there is still time to act on them. In open ground that might be many tens of hectares; in blowdown, brush or steep terrain it might be very few. Planners typically consult the hasty teams' reconnaissance before finalizing segment sizes, because the map never shows how bad the undergrowth really is. Linear features — the trails, roads and streams that lost people follow — are usually carved out as their own segments, since they are searched by different tactics at different speeds than area segments.

Each segment gets a unique identifier, and the segment map becomes the incident's central ledger. To it the planning section attaches, per segment, the POA — regional POA is subdivided among the segments within a region, often weighted by judgment about which parts of the region are likelier — the terrain and vegetation notes, hazards, access points, and the entire search history: which resource searched it, when, by what tactic, with what estimated probability of detection. Status boards or software display segments color-coded by cumulative coverage, and the classic wall map with acetate overlays survives because it lets an incoming manager absorb the whole state of the search in one look.

Two subtleties deserve mention. First, segments should be planned with the resource in mind: dog teams want segments oriented so they can work into the wind, aircraft want sweeps aligned with terrain, and trackers want corridors along travel routes rather than blocks. Second, the highest-probability segments are not automatically searched first in all cases; assignment optimizes probability of success per hour, which weighs POA against how quickly and how well a segment can be searched — a slightly lower-probability segment that is fast and easy may deliver more expected success today than a jungle of deadfall with a higher number attached. That optimization is the subject of the next section's arithmetic.

sections.heading: Probability of Detection, Coverage and the Arithmetic of Success
sections.body:
Searching a segment does not guarantee seeing what is in it, and the discipline of admitting that numerically is what separates modern search planning from wishful thinking. The key quantity is probability of detection, POD: given that the subject or clue is in the segment, the probability that this search of it would have found them. POD depends on the sensor — human eyes, dog nose, thermal camera — on the target, conscious and shouting versus unresponsive under a log, and on conditions: vegetation, light, weather, searcher spacing, fatigue. The same segment searched by the same team can honestly rate sixty percent for a responsive adult and fifteen percent for an unresponsive child, and good debriefs record PODs per target type for exactly that reason.

The intellectual foundation comes from operations research born in the Second World War, when Bernard Koopman's work on hunting submarines produced formal search theory. Its most useful gift to land search is the effort-based view of detection: define sweep width as a measure of how detectable a target is to a given sensor in given conditions — effectively the width of the strip a searcher truly clears as they move — and define coverage as effort delivered divided by area. Detection then follows a curve of diminishing returns: the exponential detection function says POD rises steeply with initial coverage and flattens as coverage grows, so pushing a segment from roughly sixty to ninety percent POD costs about as much again as getting to sixty did. Experiments — including the sweep-width trials run for land search in the 2000s that adapted the maritime methodology to ground searchers — put real numbers behind what searchers feel: detectability in open forest is many times what it is in brush, and small clues have tiny sweep widths compared to a person.

The planning payoff is the third quantity, probability of success: POS equals POA times POD. A segment with thirty percent POA searched to fifty percent POD yields fifteen points of POS — a better hour's work than a ninety percent POD search of a five percent segment. Ranking candidate assignments by expected POS per hour of resource time is the rational core of tasking, and it explains the practical wisdom of searching several likely segments to moderate POD before grinding any one segment to near-certainty.

After each assignment, the bookkeeping updates. Cumulative POD across repeated searches of a segment combines as one minus the product of the misses: two independent fifty percent searches leave a twenty-five percent chance of having missed a present subject, for a cumulative seventy-five. And unsuccessful search shifts probability: by Bayes, a segment searched without a find has its POA reduced in proportion to how good the search was, with the removed probability redistributed across the rest of the map, including rest of world. This is how the map's numbers drift, correctly, toward the places nobody has looked — including the possibility that the subject was never inside the boundary at all.

Two cultural cautions guard the arithmetic. Debriefed PODs are estimates by tired humans and run optimistic; many teams deliberately train to justify their number against spacing, speed and conditions, and managers discount bravado. And no segment is ever certified empty — the phrase searched with negative results, at an estimated POD, is the only honest statement, which is why high-probability segments are re-searched, with different resources and fresh eyes, as a search extends.

sections.heading: Choosing Tactics — Grids, Corridors, Dogs, Trackers and Aircraft
sections.body:
Tactics are the vocabulary of the operations section, and the planner's craft is matching each segment and scenario with the tactic that buys the most detection per hour. Land search doctrine commonly sorts ground tactics into three broad types. Type I, the hasty search, has already been described: fast, skilled pairs and trios working trails, drainages, hazards and likely spots, maximizing speed over thoroughness in the golden hours. Type II, often called an open or loose grid, puts a team on line through a segment at wide spacing — spacing chosen by the critical separation idea, roughly the distance at which an object like the subject remains reliably detectable between searchers — trading some thoroughness for several times the area per hour. Type III, the tight grid, is the slow, close-spaced line search that approaches high POD for small clues and unresponsive subjects; it is enormously expensive in personnel, flattens sign, and is reserved for small, critical areas — the last known cell fix, an evidence search — rather than used as a default, though it remains the image of searching the public holds.

Specialist resources multiply what ground pounders can do. Trained dog teams come in flavors that planners must not confuse. Air-scent dogs work off-lead through a segment, ranging for any human scent on the wind; they are area resources, best assigned segments they can work upwind, in conditions — cool, moist, breezy — that carry scent, and an air-scent dog can honestly deliver the coverage of many human searchers. Trailing and tracking dogs instead follow the specific scent of the subject from the PLS using a scent article; they are direction-of-travel resources whose value decays as the trail ages and the scene gets trampled, which is why they belong in the reflex phase. Human trackers, meanwhile, read physical sign — tread, transfer, crushed vegetation — and their disciplined methods, sign cutting across probable corridors to find the track and then step-by-step following, can turn a single verified print into a moving LKP that drags the whole probability map along the subject's actual route.

Aircraft add reach. Helicopters and fixed-wing sweeps cover open terrain, water margins, cliffs and alpine zones quickly, and thermal imaging at night or dawn can detect a warm subject in cover that defeats eyes — with the standing caveats that thermal is blocked by canopy and confused by sun-warmed rock, and that air search over timber has historically low POD for a stationary person. Small drones have become standard: cheap eyes over cliffs, riverbanks and blowdown too dangerous or slow for teams, imagery that can be re-examined, and thermal payloads for night work. Mounted teams, mountain bikes and vehicles patrol roads and long corridors; swiftwater and dive teams take the water margins and pools when scenarios point there; night operations, with lights and quiet listening stops, exploit the hours when a responsive subject is most likely to see and hear searchers and least likely to be moving.

Across all tactics runs one intent worth restating: search is a clue-driven, mostly non-thorough activity by design. The plan deliberately spends most hours at moderate POD across many probable places, holding the brutal thoroughness of Type III for the few spots that evidence has earned. Teams are briefed to search for the whole clue spectrum — prints, candy wrappers, scuffs, answers to calls — because finding where the subject was is the fastest route to where the subject is.

sections.heading: Assignments, Briefing and Debriefing — the Field Half of the Cycle
sections.body:
Planning becomes searching through the assignment: a written task that marries one resource to one piece of the problem for one work period. Mature searches use standard forms — in ICS-based systems, the assignment rides on a task or ICS-204-style sheet — specifying the team designation and members, the segment or route with a map, the tactic and intended thoroughness, the specific objectives including clue types sought, radio channels and reporting schedule, transport, and the expected duration. Writing it down is not bureaucracy for its own sake: the sheet is what makes the later coverage claim auditable, and it is what a replacement operations chief reads at shift change to know what was actually asked of whom.

The briefing turns the sheet into shared understanding, and its quality measurably changes search outcomes, because teams find what they are primed to find. A competent briefing covers the situation — who is missing, the story so far, the current best scenarios; the subject profile in searchable terms: clothing colors, boot sole pattern, gear that might be dropped, whether the subject will answer calls, medical issues that change what searchers should expect; the assignment itself, walked through on the map with boundaries, access, and adjacent teams named; clue awareness, including the instruction to protect and report rather than collect; communications — channels, scheduled check-ins, and the exact procedure if the subject or a major clue is found, including the discipline of confirming and securing rather than broadcasting names in the clear; and safety: terrain hazards, weather windows, turnaround times, and the reminder that no assignment justifies a searcher casualty. Good briefers close by asking the team to restate the task, because misunderstanding survives one-way speech.

Debriefing, when the team returns, is where the planning cycle actually earns its data, and it deserves the same formality as the briefing. The debriefer — ideally someone from planning, not just a sign-in table — walks the team through their actual route on the map, which in the GPS era means downloading tracks and overlaying them on the segment: the recorded track frequently shows honest gaps, drifted boundaries and unsearched corners that memory smooths over. The debrief captures conditions — visibility, wind for scent, noise from a river that defeated voice contact; the tactic actually used and the spacing actually held; every clue seen, including the ambiguous ones teams are tempted to omit; hazards discovered; and the team's own estimate of POD for a responsive and an unresponsive subject, challenged gently against their spacing and speed until the number is defensible. It also records the team's condition and availability, because tomorrow's plan is built tonight.

Two failure modes deserve naming. The first is the vanishing debrief: tired teams drift to their cars, and by morning the operations picture is a collage of guesses; the countermeasure is procedural — no team is released until debriefed, and food is at the debrief table. The second is clue mishandling: a found item picked up and passed around loses its position, its context and much of its evidentiary value; the countermeasure is the briefed rule to mark, photograph, protect, report, and touch nothing without instruction.

Assignment, briefing, debriefing: this loop is the search's metabolism. Everything the mathematics needs — PODs, tracks, clues, eliminated ground — enters the plan through the debrief table, and a search that briefs and debriefs sloppily is flying on instruments it has unplugged.

sections.heading: Operational Periods, ICS and the Planning P
sections.body:
Searches that outlast the first frantic hours need a management skeleton, and in North America and increasingly worldwide that skeleton is the Incident Command System, ICS. Born out of the 1970s California wildfire seasons, when overlapping agencies discovered their radios, ranks and terminologies could not interoperate, ICS provides a common structure now applied to any incident: one incident commander or unified command holding overall authority; an operations section that executes; a planning section that tracks resources and situation and drafts the next plan; a logistics section that feeds, fuels and equips; and finance and administration where scale demands it. Two ICS habits matter most on searches. Span of control keeps any leader supervising roughly three to seven direct reports, so a two-hundred-person search becomes a tree of teams and strike groups rather than a mob. And common terminology — plain language, standard position titles, standard forms — lets a dog team from one county, a helicopter from the state and a volunteer unit from across the border plug into the same incident without translation.

ICS organizes time as deliberately as it organizes people. The incident is cut into operational periods — commonly twelve hours on searches, sometimes shorter early when the tempo is high — and each period runs on an incident action plan, the IAP: the objectives for the period, the assignments, the communications plan, the medical plan for searchers, weather, and safety messages, assembled from standard forms. The rhythm that produces each IAP is taught as the planning P: from initial response, the cycle proceeds through gathering situation and resource status, an objectives meeting where command states what this period must achieve, a tactics meeting where operations and planning turn objectives into assignments, the planning meeting that blesses the package, IAP preparation and approval, an operational briefing to the assembled teams, and then execution — during which assessment is already feeding the next loop around the P. On a search, the search-specific mathematics — POA updates from debriefs, POS rankings for candidate assignments — slots into the tactics meeting, which is where the statistical machinery and the ICS machinery mesh.

The operational period boundary is the search's heartbeat and its most dangerous moment. Shift change is when information is lost: the outgoing operations chief knows which team was flagging, which segment boundary confused everyone, which clue smelled wrong, and unless transfer of command is done deliberately — face to face, over the map, with the documentation current — the incoming shift starts the cycle partly blind. Well-run searches protect the handover ruthlessly and keep the planning section slightly out of phase with operations, planning tomorrow while today executes, so no period begins without a plan already printed.

ICS also carries functions searches need but planners forget. A safety officer with authority to stop unsafe operations. A public information officer, because missing person searches attract cameras and social media speculation that can flood the incident with false sightings — which still must be logged and graded. A family liaison, keeping the family informed and interviewed with dignity, away from the operational floor. And documentation throughout, because searches end in coroner's inquests, lawsuits and after-action reviews, and the incident that cannot show its reasoning on paper will be judged by hindsight alone.

The deeper point is that ICS and the search planning cycle are not rivals but gears: ICS turns the organizational wheel — periods, plans, briefings — and the search cycle turns inside it, updating belief and effort. Small searches run both loops informally in one leader's head; the structure exists so that nothing breaks when the incident grows a hundredfold overnight.

sections.heading: Clue Management — Running the Search on Evidence
sections.body:
A search generates clues faster than it generates subjects, and the discipline of handling them — capturing, grading, mapping, and acting on them — is called clue management. The doctrine rests on a simple biological fact: a person moving through landscape sheds evidence continuously. Footprints at a rate of hundreds per kilometer, scent, disturbed vegetation, fibers on brush, dropped and discarded objects, fire rings, shelters, answers shouted back at night, sightings by other humans. The subject is one target; their clues are thousands of targets, each larger in aggregate than the person, and every verified clue collapses the search area toward the subject's actual path. The maxim taught to every new searcher is blunt: you may walk past the subject once, but you will walk past clues all day — so search for clues.

Management begins with capture. Teams are briefed to detect, protect and report: stop, mark the location without trampling the surroundings, photograph in place with something for scale, record coordinates, and call it in — not to collect, because an object in a pocket has lost its position, orientation and context, and because some searches become crime scenes retroactively, at which point chain of custody matters. The incident maintains a clue log — every report numbered, time-stamped, located and attributed — and a clue officer or the planning section owns it. Nothing reported is beneath logging: the cigarette brand that matches the subject, the candy wrapper that does not, the print that turns out to be a searcher's. Even eliminated clues are kept, because elimination is information and because patterns emerge across a log that no single team can see.

Each clue is then assessed on two axes: is it connected to the subject, and what does it imply if so? Connection is tested against the profile — sole pattern against the boots the spouse described, size against the subject's feet, the dropped glove shown to family, freshness judged by weathering. Searches grade clues into rough classes from confirmed through probable to possible and unrelated, and the grade governs how much the plan is allowed to move: a confirmed clue can relocate the IPP and trigger a full re-plan; a possible clue redirects a team to investigate but does not yet bend the probability map. The classic failure here is clue seduction — the whole incident lurching after an exciting object that was never the subject's — and the antidote is the written grade with its reasoning, plus the standing rest-of-world humility.

Acted upon, clues become tactics. A confirmed track launches trackers on step-by-step and re-centers segments along the direction of travel. A reliable sighting redraws POA around a new point with a new time. A pattern of clues along a drainage converts scattered probability into a corridor. Negative clue traps work too: track traps established across egress routes that stay clean, and doors that stay unopened, quietly eliminate scenarios in the log.

The subtle categories deserve care. Sightings from the public arrive in bulk once media cover a search, and each must be logged, graded for reliability, and where possible tested — what was the person wearing, from how far, in what light — because a single mis-graded sighting has derailed major searches for days. Electronic clues — phone pings, payment card use, smart-device locations — arrive through investigation and often outrank anything physical. And absence itself is a clue: the shelter that shows no one entered, the register unsigned. A search that manages its clues is reasoning; one that does not is merely walking.

sections.heading: Scaling Back, Suspension and Learning From the Search
sections.body:
Most searches end quickly and well: the majority of subjects are located within the first day or two, many by the reflex tasks. But some do not, and the planning cycle must govern the hardest phase — deciding how long to continue at full effort, how to scale down defensibly, and how to close an incident that has not found its subject, without abandoning the family or the truth.

The decision framework is explicit. Continued full-scale effort is justified while there is searchable probability: significant POA remaining in segments that have not been searched to reasonable cumulative POD, live scenarios not yet run to ground, and a realistic chance of survival. Each planning meeting in an extended search therefore reviews three ledgers. The coverage ledger: cumulative POD by segment, and what the Bayesian shifts have done to the map — is the remaining probability concentrated anywhere actionable, or smeared thinly everywhere and into rest of world? The scenario ledger: which stories remain alive, and what specific tasks would kill or confirm them? The survivability ledger: given the elapsed time, weather actually endured, the subject's age, condition, clothing and access to water, what do the survival models and medical advisors say — remembering the humbling record of subjects found alive after many days, which is why survivability informs but never solely dictates the decision.

Scaling back is a spectrum, not a switch. Searches step down from continuous operations to daylight-only, from mass resources to specialist teams re-searching the highest remaining segments — different eyes and sensors on the same ground, because cumulative POD arithmetic rewards independent looks. A widely used posture is limited continuous search: the incident formally demobilizes, but specific tasks continue — patrols of travel routes, periodic checks of track traps and attraction points, dog teams on high-value segments in good scent conditions, aircraft passes when other missions overfly the area. Investigation typically continues longest, because the phone records, the bank card, and the tip from a distant town cost little and retain real probability of resolution.

Formal suspension, when it comes, is a command decision made with documented reasoning, reviewed by the responsible agency, and communicated to the family before the press — face to face, by someone senior, with an honest account of what was done, what the probabilities now say, and exactly what will trigger reactivation: a new clue, a seasonal change such as snowmelt exposing ground, a hunter's report. Suspension is not closure; reactivation criteria keep the case alive administratively, and many long-missing subjects are eventually found by the public, whose reports the agency must remain organized to receive and grade.

When the objective changes from rescue to recovery — a live-find dog alerting on a debris pile no one could survive, evidence of entry into water in flood — the incident acknowledges it explicitly, because tactics change: recovery justifies slower, higher-POD methods, different specialist resources, and different risk calculus, since no searcher should accept rescue-level risk for a recovery.

Finally, every significant search should end in an after-action review: what the initial report got wrong, which scenario the clues actually supported, where the segment boundaries failed, how the PODs compared with the find location when there was one, and what the incident will change next time. The lost person behavior statistics that opened this guide exist because past searches submitted their data honestly. Feeding the case back into that record — through debrief archives and incident databases — is the last turn of the planning cycle, the one that makes the next search for the next missing stranger a little shorter.

guides.safetyNote: Searching is hazardous work. Searchers operate in the same terrain, weather, darkness and water that got the subject into trouble, often while tired and emotionally involved. Never self-deploy to a search; work only under the incident organization, stay with your assigned team, carry the clothing, food, water and light to look after yourself for a full operational period, and turn back or call for help the moment conditions exceed your training. A searcher who becomes a casualty takes resources away from the person who is already missing. This guide describes planning concepts for education; formal search management and field skills require training and practice with a recognized team, and in a real emergency you should immediately call the local emergency number rather than organizing a private search.

guides.title: Incident Command System for Rescue
guides.summary: How the Incident Command System organises people, equipment and information at a rescue — its five functions, span of control, the Incident Action Plan and planning cycle, communications and accountability — and how to run a scaled-down version of it at a small incident with untrained help.

sections.heading: Why a Rescue Needs a Command Structure at All
sections.body:
A rescue is a problem of coordination at least as much as it is a problem of technique. The rope work, the medicine, the searching and the extrication are all learnable skills, and the people who arrive at an incident usually possess a reasonable amount of them. What routinely fails is everything that sits between those skills and the outcome: who is doing what, who knows what, who is allowed to decide, and whether anyone has counted the rescuers recently. Reviews of failed operations in wildland fire, mountain rescue, urban search and rescue, and mass-casualty medicine converge on the same short list of causes, and technical incompetence is rarely at the top of it. Duplicated effort, unassigned critical tasks, radios that cannot talk to each other, freelancing individuals who nobody can locate, and a commander drowning in twenty simultaneous conversations appear far more often.

The Incident Command System, universally abbreviated ICS, is a standard answer to that coordination problem. It is a management structure — a way of arranging people and information — that can be applied to any incident of any size, in any discipline, by any combination of agencies. It says nothing about how to tie a knot or splint a femur. It says a great deal about how to make sure that the person who can tie the knot has been told where to go, has a radio channel that works, has been logged in so somebody notices if they do not come back, and is operating under an objective that somebody in a position to see the whole picture actually set.

Its central insight is that management capacity is a consumable resource, exactly like rope or oxygen, and that it is exhausted much earlier than most people expect. A single competent person can direct perhaps three to seven others effectively. Beyond that, quality of supervision collapses rapidly: instructions get shorter and vaguer, feedback stops flowing upward, and the supervisor's attention becomes entirely reactive. ICS treats this limit as a hard engineering constraint and builds an organisation that grows by adding layers of supervision rather than by piling more people onto one overloaded individual.

The second insight is that a structure invented during an emergency will be invented badly. Under stress, groups default to whoever is loudest, most senior in ordinary life, or first on scene, and those are poor proxies for who should be running things. Having a pre-agreed structure that everyone has trained on removes an entire category of argument at the worst possible moment. When a paramedic, a police sergeant and a volunteer team leader all arrive at a riverbank within four minutes of each other, ICS gives them a shared, rehearsed answer to the question of what happens next, and that shared answer is worth more than any one of them being individually right.

sections.heading: Origins: FIRESCOPE, the 1970 Fires, and the Road to NIMS
sections.body:
The Incident Command System was born out of a specific catastrophe. In late September and October 1970, a series of wildfires driven by Santa Ana winds burned across southern California. Over roughly thirteen days, some 773 separate fires consumed on the order of 600,000 acres, destroyed around 700 structures and killed sixteen people. Enormous quantities of firefighting resources were committed. The subsequent analysis found that the losses were not principally caused by a shortage of engines, crews or aircraft. They were caused by the inability of dozens of federal, state, county and municipal agencies to work as a single organisation. Agencies used different terminology for the same equipment, could not communicate by radio, had incompatible chains of command, and produced no shared plan. Requests for help went unanswered because nobody knew who was authorised to answer them.

Congress funded a research programme in response, and in 1972 a consortium called FIRESCOPE — Firefighting Resources of California Organized for Potential Emergencies — began developing a common command structure and a multi-agency coordination system. The work took most of the decade. What emerged was deliberately generic: a set of functions rather than a set of fire-specific procedures, using plain terminology, modular expansion, and standard forms. By the early 1980s the National Wildfire Coordinating Group had folded FIRESCOPE's product into the National Interagency Incident Management System, and ICS began migrating out of wildland fire into structural firefighting, hazardous materials response, law enforcement and emergency medical services.

The decisive push into universal adoption in the United States came after the attacks of 11 September 2001. The 9/11 Commission's findings on the response at the World Trade Center described exactly the failure modes FIRESCOPE had been created to fix, thirty years later and in a different discipline: separate police and fire command posts, incompatible radios, and no unified accountability for who was inside the buildings. Homeland Security Presidential Directive 5, issued in February 2003, directed the creation of the National Incident Management System, and NIMS made ICS the required incident management structure for any organisation receiving federal preparedness funding. Adoption became effectively mandatory across American emergency services.

Parallel and largely compatible systems developed elsewhere. The United Kingdom's Joint Emergency Services Interoperability Principles, Australasia's AIIMS, and Canada's provincial ICS variants all share the same functional skeleton, with differences mostly in vocabulary — the UK's gold, silver and bronze command tiers, for example, map recognisably onto strategic, tactical and task levels. For a rescuer, the practical consequence is that the vocabulary in this guide will be understood, with minor translation, almost anywhere professional response happens. That interoperability was the entire point, and it was bought with the losses of 1970.

sections.heading: The Five Functions That Every Incident Requires
sections.body:
ICS rests on the claim that every incident, from a single lost hiker to a regional flood, requires the same five things to be done, and that the only variable is how many people are needed to do them. Those five functions are Command, Operations, Planning, Logistics, and Finance and Administration. At a tiny incident one person performs all five and probably does not name them. At a large one, each becomes a section with a chief, a staff and its own internal subdivisions. The functions do not appear and disappear; only their staffing changes.

Command sets objectives, establishes priorities, and holds overall responsibility. The Incident Commander decides what the operation is trying to achieve — locate and extract the casualty from the ravine before dark, contain the spill before it reaches the storm drain — and owns the consequences. Command is the one function that always exists and is always filled by exactly one person or one unified team; it is never vacant.

Operations does the tactical work. Everyone with hands on the problem sits under Operations: the rope team on the edge, the medics at the casualty, the searchers on the ridge, the pump crew. Operations is almost always the largest section and consumes the most resources. A useful test of whether a task belongs to Operations is whether it directly advances an incident objective; if it does, it is operational, and if it merely supports someone who does, it is logistics.

Planning collects and evaluates information, tracks where every resource is, and produces the written plan for the next operating period. It is the section people most often skip and most often regret skipping, because it is the only one whose product is a shared picture of reality. Planning also owns demobilisation — the orderly release of resources — which is where a surprising fraction of injuries occur, as tired people drive home from incidents that nobody formally ended.

Logistics obtains and provides everything the responders need to function: food, water, fuel, lighting, shelter, medical care for responders, ground support, and above all communications. Logistics is a service function, not a tactical one; its customers are the responders, not the victims. A frequent early failure at long incidents is that nobody stands Logistics up, so the Operations Section Chief spends the first three hours chasing batteries instead of directing rescue.

Finance and Administration tracks cost, time, procurement and claims. At a two-hour rescue this is trivial and is absorbed by Command. At a multi-day incident with contracted helicopters, injured volunteers, and damaged private property, it becomes essential, and the records it keeps determine whether an agency is reimbursed and whether an injured responder's claim succeeds. Its unglamorous documentation is what makes the operation survivable afterwards.

sections.heading: Span of Control and the Modular Organisation
sections.body:
The load-bearing constraint in the whole system is span of control: the number of subordinates a single supervisor can direct effectively. ICS sets this at three to seven, with five as the planning target, and treats an excursion beyond seven as a defect requiring immediate correction rather than as an inconvenience to be tolerated. The number is not arbitrary. It comes from a long line of research on human attention and supervision, and it degrades sharply with stress, noise, fatigue and radio-mediated rather than face-to-face communication — all of which describe a rescue exactly. In a quiet office ten reports may be manageable. On a windy hillside at night, over a shared radio channel, with a hypothermic casualty and failing light, the effective ceiling is closer to four.

The consequence is that ICS grows downward, not outward. When a supervisor's span exceeds seven, the organisation does not respond by asking that person to try harder. It responds by inserting a layer: subordinates are grouped, a supervisor is appointed for each group, and the original supervisor now directs three or four supervisors instead of twelve individuals. This is what "modular" means in ICS literature. The structure expands and contracts by adding and removing whole modules, each of which has a defined name, a defined supervisor title, and a defined reporting line.

The reverse operation matters just as much and is neglected far more often. As an incident winds down, layers should be collapsed and positions absorbed back upward, so that a shrinking operation is not still being run by a fifteen-person overhead team. Failing to demobilise the structure keeps people on scene who are tired, bored and increasingly likely to make mistakes, and it burns money and goodwill that the organisation will need next time.

A related discipline is that positions, not people, are the units of organisation. ICS names roles — Operations Section Chief, Division A Supervisor, Medical Unit Leader — and those roles exist independently of who is filling them. This allows relief, shift change and escalation without renegotiating the structure, and it means radio traffic can be addressed to a function rather than to a name. Calling for "Division B" reaches whoever currently holds that post, which is exactly what the caller needs; calling for "Sarah" fails the moment Sarah hands over.

One nuance worth stating plainly: span of control applies to supervisory relationships, not to headcount. A Division Supervisor directing four crew leaders, each of whom leads five people, is supervising four, not twenty, and is within limits. The error to watch for is the supervisor who has nominally delegated but is in practice still talking directly to every individual, which produces the appearance of a correct chart and the reality of an overloaded person. If a supervisor's radio never stops, span has collapsed regardless of what the chart says.

sections.heading: Assuming, Transferring and Delegating Command
sections.body:
Command must be established explicitly, out loud, and early. The convention is that the first competent responder on scene assumes command and announces it — "Engine 4 is on scene, establishing Riverside Command" — and then keeps it until it is formally transferred. This matters because the alternative, an incident where everyone assumes somebody else is in charge, is the default failure state of an unmanaged emergency. The announcement is not a claim of expertise; it is a claim of responsibility, and it can be made by a relatively junior person. A firefighter, a nurse or a trained volunteer can and should take command of a scene until relieved.

Transfer of command happens for four legitimate reasons: a more qualified person arrives, jurisdiction changes, the incident grows or shrinks enough to warrant a different level of management, or the current commander needs relief from fatigue. It should never happen simply because someone more senior in ordinary organisational rank turns up. A chief officer arriving at a technical rope rescue does not automatically become the best person to command it, and the professional norm in most rescue disciplines is that the more qualified person takes command only if they are more qualified for this incident.

The transfer itself must be a face-to-face briefing wherever physically possible, and it should cover a defined set of items: the current situation and what has changed, the objectives in force, the current organisation and who holds which position, the resources assigned and their locations, the resources ordered and en route, known hazards and safety concerns, and any decisions the incoming commander needs to make immediately. Only when that briefing is complete does the incoming commander announce assumption of command over the radio, so that everyone knows the address has changed. A transfer that happens silently, or that consists of "you've got it", reliably produces an hour of confusion afterwards.

Delegation of authority is the third piece and is frequently misunderstood. An Incident Commander cannot delegate responsibility — they remain accountable for the outcome — but they must delegate authority, meaning the power to make decisions within a defined scope. A Division Supervisor who has been told to search a drainage but who must radio for permission before moving a team fifty metres is not being supervised, they are being remote-controlled, and the commander who insists on that will saturate within twenty minutes. The workable norm is to delegate by objective: state what the subordinate is to achieve, what constraints apply, what they may not do without asking, and then leave them alone unless something changes. In some jurisdictions, particularly for complex or long-duration incidents, this is formalised in a written Delegation of Authority letter from the agency administrator to the Incident Commander, defining the commander's limits on spending, on committing agency assets, and on interacting with the press. For a two-hour rescue the same content is conveyed in a sentence, but the substance is identical: everyone must know the edge of their own discretion.

sections.heading: Unity of Command, Unified Command, and Multi-Agency Coordination
sections.body:
Two similar-sounding terms carry entirely different meanings, and confusing them causes real problems. Unity of command is the principle that every individual reports to exactly one supervisor and receives orders from exactly one source. Unified command is a structure in which several agencies jointly hold the Incident Commander role.

Unity of command is non-negotiable and applies at every level. Its violation is the single most common cause of chaos on multi-agency scenes: a rescuer receives one instruction from the person supervising them and a contradictory one from someone from their own parent organisation who happens to walk past with more stripes. The rule is that once you are assigned, your supervisor is your supervisor, regardless of who employs you, and instructions from anyone else are politely deflected to that supervisor. Enforcing this takes courage, because it means a volunteer telling a senior officer from their own service that they cannot take that instruction, but a structure where it is not enforced is decorative.

Unified command exists because many incidents involve agencies with genuinely separate legal responsibilities that cannot be surrendered. A rescue from a road-traffic collision involving a chemical load may sit simultaneously under a fire service with a statutory duty for rescue, a police service with a duty to investigate and preserve evidence, an ambulance service with a duty of care to patients, and an environmental regulator with a duty over the watercourse. None of those can lawfully hand its mandate to another. Unified command resolves this by having those agencies' commanders form a single command team, physically co-located, that jointly sets one set of objectives and approves one Incident Action Plan. Below that team, the organisation is entirely normal: there is still exactly one Operations Section Chief, and every responder still has one supervisor.

The crucial discipline in unified command is that the team produces a single set of objectives, not three parallel plans stapled together. Where objectives conflict — police wanting an untouched scene, ambulance wanting rapid access to a patient — the team negotiates a priority order in the command post rather than letting the conflict be resolved by whichever crew reaches the vehicle first. Life safety conventionally outranks evidence preservation, and saying so explicitly in the objectives prevents an argument at the casualty's side.

Above the incident sits multi-agency coordination: emergency operations centres, coordination groups and policy bodies that support the incident with resources, set regional priorities between competing incidents, and handle the political and public-information load. These bodies do not command the incident. The distinction is worth defending, because an emergency operations centre that starts directing tactics has silently created a second chain of command, violating unity of command at the highest possible level and producing exactly the confusion the whole system exists to prevent.

sections.heading: Inside Operations: Divisions, Groups, Branches and Task Forces
sections.body:
The Operations Section is where rescue actually happens, and its internal vocabulary is precise in ways that repay learning, because these words are how work gets addressed on the radio.

A Division is a geographic subdivision. It covers an area — a slope, a floor of a building, a river reach, a quadrant of a search area — and everyone working in that area reports to its Supervisor. Conventions differ by discipline: structural firefighting labels building sides A through D clockwise from the front and floors by number, wildland fire uses letters running clockwise around the perimeter, and search operations usually number segments from a map. The point is not which convention you use but that everyone on the incident uses the same one.

A Group is a functional subdivision. It performs a particular kind of work wherever that work is needed: a Medical Group, a Rope Group, a Ventilation Group, a Litter Group. Groups cross division boundaries. When a Group and a Division operate in the same physical space, they are peers and must coordinate directly with each other; neither commands the other. This peer relationship is a common source of friction and needs to be stated in briefings.

A Branch sits above divisions and groups and exists for one of three reasons: span of control at the division level has been exceeded, the incident has functionally distinct halves that need separate management, or several agencies need parallel structures. A large flood rescue might run a Water Rescue Branch and an Evacuation Branch, each with several divisions beneath it. Branches are the mechanism by which Operations grows past about seven subordinate elements without breaking span of control.

Single resources, task forces and strike teams are the units of assignment. A single resource is one piece of equipment with its crew, or one individual. A strike team is a set of resources of the same kind and type — five identical engines, four identical swiftwater teams — with common communications and a leader. A task force is a mixed set assembled for a specific job, again with common communications and a leader. Both exist principally to reduce span of control: an Operations Section Chief who orders five task forces is managing five things, not twenty-five.

Two more elements deserve mention. Staging is a location where assigned but uncommitted resources wait, under a Staging Area Manager, ready to move within a defined time — commonly three minutes in structural response. Staging is what stops a scene from being clogged with idle people and vehicles, and it is one of the highest-value moves a commander can make in the first ten minutes of a growing incident. Air Operations, where aircraft are involved, is normally a branch of its own with dedicated frequencies and a supervisor whose sole job is deconfliction, because a helicopter operating without positive control over a rope system or a hillside of searchers is a lethal hazard rather than a resource.

sections.heading: Objectives, Strategy, Tactics, and the SMART Test
sections.body:
The chain that converts a commander's intent into someone's hands on a rope runs through three levels, and confusing them is one of the most reliable ways to produce a badly run incident.

Objectives are what is to be achieved. They belong to Command, they are written down, and they are set for a defined operating period. A well-formed objective states an outcome and a condition, not a method. "Locate the missing walker within the eastern drainage by 2200" is an objective. "Send two teams up the east ridge" is not; that is a tactic that has been mistaken for one. The distinction matters enormously, because objectives that specify method strip subordinate supervisors of the discretion they need and simultaneously commit the incident to an approach before anyone has evaluated alternatives.

Strategy is the broad approach chosen to meet an objective — search the drainage from the bottom up using hasty teams on the trails first, then grid the brush — and typically belongs to the Operations Section Chief in consultation with Planning. Tactics are the specific assignments given to specific resources to execute the strategy, and belong to division and group supervisors. Each level is set by the level above and executed with discretion by the level below.

Objectives are conventionally tested against the SMART criteria: specific, measurable, attainable, relevant and time-bound. Applied honestly this is a demanding filter. "Ensure scene safety" fails on measurability — you cannot tell whether it has been achieved. "Establish and maintain a hot-zone perimeter of at least fifty metres, with entry control, by 1430" passes. "Rescue all casualties immediately" fails on attainability if you have four casualties in a confined space and one rescue team.
