Writing an unattainable objective is not harmless optimism; it guarantees the operating period ends in apparent failure and it removes the commander's ability to prioritise, because everything is equally urgent.

Objectives must also be prioritised, not merely listed. The conventional ordering in almost every rescue discipline is life safety first, incident stabilisation second, property and environmental conservation third. Within life safety, responder safety is placed ahead of victim safety, which sounds cold and is in fact the only defensible position: a rescuer who becomes a casualty converts one problem into two and consumes the resources that would have solved the first. Making this ordering explicit in the written objectives gives subordinates a decision rule for the moment when they cannot do everything.

Finally, the number of objectives should be small. Three to five for an operating period is normal and ten is a symptom of a commander who has not decided anything. A list of everything that would be nice to accomplish is not a plan; it is a wish, and it delegates the actual prioritisation downward to whoever happens to be holding the radio, which is precisely the failure the system was built to prevent.

sections.heading: The Operating Period and the Planning Cycle
sections.body:
An incident that lasts more than a few hours has to be managed in chunks, and the chunk in ICS is called the operating period. It is a defined block of time — commonly twelve hours for large incidents, often two to four hours in the early volatile phase, and sometimes as short as the daylight remaining — for which one set of objectives is in force and one plan is written. Operating periods are chosen to fit natural boundaries: daylight and darkness, tide, shift change, forecast weather. Nothing about the incident stops at the boundary; what changes is that the objectives are formally reviewed and a new plan is issued.

The reason for imposing this rhythm is that continuous replanning is indistinguishable from having no plan. If objectives can change at any moment, subordinates cannot commit to anything, resources cannot be ordered with confidence, and nobody ever knows whether the last thing they heard is still current. Fixing the plan for a stated period buys stability, and stability is what allows a Division Supervisor to actually get something finished.

The cycle that produces each plan is taught in ICS as the Planning P, so named because the sequence drawn on paper forms a leg and a loop. The leg is the one-off start of the incident: notification, initial response and assessment, the first incident briefing, and the initial Incident Commander's decision on objectives. The loop then repeats once per operating period. Its stages are, in order: an Incident Command and General Staff meeting; preparing for the tactics meeting; the tactics meeting itself, where Operations and Planning work out what will actually be done and with what; preparing for the planning meeting; the planning meeting, where the proposed plan is presented to the commander for approval; plan preparation and approval; the operational period briefing, where the plan is handed to the people who will execute it; and finally execution, assessment of progress, and the start of the next turn of the loop.

Two products anchor the middle of that loop. The first is the operational planning worksheet, ICS Form 215, on which Operations lays out each division and group, the work to be done, and the resources required — which immediately exposes any gap between what is wanted and what exists. The second is the safety analysis, ICS Form 215A, in which the Safety Officer works down the same list of assignments identifying hazards and required mitigations. Doing these two in parallel, on the same structure, is what forces safety to be considered assignment by assignment rather than as a generic exhortation.

Timing discipline makes or breaks the cycle. Each meeting has a scheduled start, a defined attendee list and a hard time limit; a planning meeting that runs long pushes plan preparation into the night and produces a briefing at which nobody has read the plan. Experienced Planning Section Chiefs guard the clock ruthlessly, publish the meeting schedule at the start of the incident, and hold it, because a rhythm everyone can rely on is worth more than a perfect plan delivered late.

sections.heading: The Incident Action Plan and Its Forms
sections.body:
The Incident Action Plan, universally called the IAP, is the written output of the planning cycle: a document, valid for one operating period, that states what will be achieved, who will do it, how they will talk to each other, what the medical arrangements are, and what the hazards are. It may be a single page or a fifty-page package. Its defining property is that it is written and distributed, so that everyone works from the same text rather than from their individual recollection of a briefing.

The core of the IAP is a small set of standard forms, and knowing what each one carries is genuinely useful even to someone who will never fill one in. ICS Form 202 is the incident objectives page, carrying the operating period, the objectives themselves, a command emphasis or safety message, and the commander's signature. ICS 203 is the organisation assignment list — the current chart in list form, naming who holds each position. ICS 204, the assignment list, is the form that matters most to working responders: there is one per division or group, and it states the resources assigned, the specific work assignment, special instructions, and the communications to be used. If a rescuer reads only one page of the IAP, it is their 204.

ICS 205 is the incident radio communications plan, listing every channel in use, its function, its frequency or talkgroup, and who is assigned to it. ICS 206 is the medical plan for responders, listing on-scene medical resources, transport, hospitals with their capabilities and distances, and the procedure for calling for help — a document whose value becomes apparent the first time a rescuer is injured at two in the morning. A map or sketch is normally attached, and 215A, the safety analysis, or a separate safety message is included.

Beyond that core, larger incidents attach a weather forecast, an air operations summary, a demobilisation plan, and traffic or access plans. Supporting forms in wide use include ICS 201, the initial incident briefing form, which is the single most useful document at a small incident because it captures the situation sketch, objectives, current organisation and resource summary on four sides of paper and doubles as the transfer-of-command briefing; ICS 211, the check-in list; ICS 213, the general message form; and ICS 214, the unit activity log, which every supervisor should keep and which becomes the evidentiary record when something is later disputed.

The approval step is not a formality. The Incident Commander signs the IAP, and in signing accepts that the plan is achievable with the resources listed and that its hazards have been addressed. A commander who signs a plan they have not read has abolished the only quality gate in the system.

sections.heading: Planning Section: Situation, Resources, Documentation, Demobilisation
sections.body:
The Planning Section exists to answer two questions continuously: what is actually happening, and where is everybody. It is the incident's memory and its map, and it is the function most often left unstaffed by teams who think of planning as paperwork rather than as situational awareness.

The Resources Unit owns accountability. It checks resources in as they arrive, records their status as assigned, available or out of service, and knows at any moment where every crew and every vehicle is and who supervises them. In many systems this is maintained physically on a T-card rack — one card per resource, moved between columns as status changes — precisely because a physical board is legible at a glance, survives power failure, and cannot silently disagree with itself. The Resources Unit is what makes it possible to answer the question that follows every close call: is everyone accounted for.

The Situation Unit owns the picture. It collects reports, maintains the incident map, produces the situation summary, and projects forward. Its most valuable product is often the simplest: a large, current, visible map with division boundaries, resource positions, hazards and the last known position of the subject marked on it. A rescue in which the map on the bonnet of a vehicle is four hours out of date is a rescue in which the commander is making decisions about a place that no longer exists. Search operations lean on this unit especially heavily, since probability of area and probability of detection calculations, and the segment-by-segment record of coverage achieved, live here.

The Documentation Unit maintains the incident file: every plan, every form, every log, every message. Its work looks bureaucratic during the incident and becomes the most important thing in the room afterwards, when a coroner, an insurer, a regulator or a learning review asks what was known and when. Rescuers who have been through a serious inquiry universally report the same lesson, which is that contemporaneous records written at the time are believed and reconstructions written afterwards are not.

The Demobilisation Unit plans the ending. Demobilisation is a genuine hazard phase: people are exhausted, the adrenaline has gone, and they are about to drive tired vehicles home on public roads. A demobilisation plan specifies release priorities, required rest before travel, equipment return and cleaning, the check-out process, and a route for people who need a debrief. Formally releasing a resource, rather than letting it drift away, is also the only way the Resources Unit can close the loop on accountability.

Planning may also host technical specialists — a hydrologist, a structural engineer, a mine rescue advisor, a cave surveyor, a canine handler coordinator. They are placed in Planning rather than Operations because their job is to inform the plan rather than to execute tasks, and because putting them in the planning meeting is what allows their expertise to shape objectives instead of merely constraining tactics after the fact.

sections.heading: Logistics and Finance: Keeping the Operation Alive
sections.body:
Logistics is the section that decides whether an incident can last. Rescues that end within two hours rarely need it; anything that runs past a shift boundary needs it badly, and the transition is usually noticed too late, at the point where the Operations Section Chief is personally hunting for radio batteries.

Logistics divides into a service branch and a support branch. The service branch runs communications, medical support for responders, and food. The Communications Unit is the most consequential: it issues radios, maintains the incident communications plan, runs the incident communications centre, and is responsible for the fact that the rope team on the cliff can actually reach the command post. Physics does not care about the organisational chart, and a unit leader who understands terrain shadowing, repeater coverage and the need for relay positions is worth an entire extra crew. The Medical Unit provides care for responders, not for victims — victim care is operational — and staffs the first-aid post, tracks responder injuries and implements the ICS 206 plan. The Food Unit sounds trivial and is not: a rescue team twelve hours into an operation without hot food or fluids is a team whose decision quality has measurably degraded, and dehydration and low blood sugar are ordinary, preventable causes of rescuer error.

The support branch handles supply, facilities and ground support. Supply orders and receives everything from batteries to litter wheels and keeps an accountable record of what was issued to whom. Facilities builds the incident base, the command post, sleeping and sanitation arrangements, and lighting. Ground support fuels, maintains and drives vehicles, and manages the transport plan — which is also, on a large incident, one of the largest sources of injury, since vehicle collisions during response and return are a leading killer of emergency responders in most national statistics.

Finance and Administration is the section that most volunteer rescuers never see and that determines whether their organisation survives the incident financially. Its Time Unit records personnel and equipment hours, which drives both reimbursement and, in paid services, payroll. The Procurement Unit handles contracts, hire agreements and vendor payments. The Compensation and Claims Unit handles two distinct streams: injury compensation for responders, and claims from members of the public for damage — a fence cut for access, a field rutted by a vehicle, a door forced. The Cost Unit tracks the running cost of the incident and provides the commander with cost estimates for proposed courses of action, which is genuinely useful decision information when the choice is between a helicopter and six more hours of ground search.

The unifying principle for both sections is that they are demand-driven services. Their job is not to ration but to anticipate: the good Logistics Section Chief has already ordered the lighting before darkness is mentioned, and the good Finance Section Chief has already opened a claims file before anyone complains about the gate.

sections.heading: The Command Staff: Safety, Public Information and Liaison
sections.body:
Three positions report directly to the Incident Commander rather than sitting inside a section, and together they are called the Command Staff. They exist because each performs work that must not be filtered through Operations, and each carries authority that would be compromised if it were.

The Safety Officer is the most important of the three and the only ICS position with authority to override the chain of command. A Safety Officer may stop or alter any operation, immediately and without prior approval, on the grounds of imminent danger to responders. That authority is deliberate and it is unique: everywhere else in the system, instructions flow down through supervisors, but a hazard that will kill someone in the next ninety seconds cannot wait for a message to travel up three levels and back down. The Safety Officer's routine work is quieter — surveying hazards, completing the safety analysis for each assignment, checking that protective equipment matches the exposure, monitoring for fatigue and heat or cold stress, and briefing the safety message that goes into the plan. On large incidents assistant safety officers are assigned to individual divisions, because one person cannot see a five-kilometre perimeter. The single best predictor of whether the position works is whether the person filling it is genuinely willing to use the stop authority in front of colleagues, which is a matter of character and organisational culture rather than of paperwork.

The Public Information Officer handles all contact with the media and with the public, and their existence protects the incident twice over. It keeps journalists and inquiring relatives away from a commander who has no spare attention, and it ensures that one accurate account is issued rather than five contradictory ones assembled from whoever a reporter caught at the cordon. In a rescue with a named missing person this role also touches the family, and in many jurisdictions family liaison is a specialised function of its own with strict rules about what may be said before formal identification. The standing rule for everyone else on scene is simple: refer all media to the PIO, decline politely, and never speculate about a casualty's condition.

The Liaison Officer is the contact point for assisting and cooperating agencies that are not part of the command structure — a utility company, a landowner, a railway operator, a charity, a neighbouring service sending resources. Without this position, representatives of those bodies gravitate naturally toward the commander and consume the scarcest attention on the incident. With it, they have somebody whose actual job is to talk to them, which is both more courteous and vastly more efficient.

At a small incident all three roles are held by the commander, and that is legitimate — but the Safety Officer is usually the first position worth splitting out, ahead even of Operations, because the commander who is directing tactics is precisely the person least able to notice that the slope above the team has started shedding rock.

sections.heading: Common Terminology, Plain Language and Radio Discipline
sections.body:
One of the quiet revolutions in ICS was the abolition of codes. Multi-agency incidents fail on vocabulary before they fail on anything else, because two services can use the same three-digit code for entirely different things and neither will realise the misunderstanding until it has consequences. NIMS and its equivalents therefore require plain language on multi-agency incidents: say "we need an ambulance" rather than a numeric signal, say "the patient has stopped breathing" rather than a service-specific abbreviation. The rule feels clumsy to experienced operators who have used codes for twenty years, and it is nonetheless correct, because it is precisely under stress and across agency boundaries that codes are misheard and misapplied.

Common terminology extends past plain language to a shared naming scheme for positions, facilities and resources. Positions have fixed titles — Chief for a section, Director for a branch, Supervisor for a division or group, Leader for a unit or task force, Manager for a facility such as staging — so that hearing a title tells you the level of the person speaking. Facilities are named consistently: Incident Command Post, Base, Camp, Staging Area, Helibase, Helispot. And resources are typed, which is the practice of grading capability numerically so that an order communicates what will actually arrive. A Type 1 resource is the most capable; a Type 4 the least. Ordering "a Type 2 swiftwater rescue team" specifies training level, equipment and staffing in three words, and the requesting commander knows what will show up on the riverbank at 0300 without a negotiation.

Radio discipline is the practical expression of all of this. The core habits are few and each fixes a specific failure. Identify by position, not name, so traffic reaches whoever holds the post. Say who you are calling before you say who you are, so the receiver knows to listen. Keep transmissions short and finish a thought before releasing the key. Use closed-loop confirmation for anything consequential — the receiver reads back the instruction, the sender confirms — which catches the misheard grid reference before the team walks two kilometres in the wrong direction. Wait a beat after pressing transmit, because most radio systems clip the first syllable while the channel opens.

Channel discipline matters as much as speech discipline. The communications plan should separate command traffic from tactical traffic and, on any incident with a technical hazard, should give the operational team working the hazard a dedicated channel that nobody else uses. A rope team and an air unit sharing a channel with a logistics conversation about fuel is a design fault, not a personality problem. Where teams from different agencies genuinely cannot interoperate on radio — different bands, different encryption, no common talkgroup — the honest fix is a human relay: a person physically positioned with two radios whose sole job is to pass traffic between systems. It is inelegant, it works, and it has saved more incidents than any procurement programme.

sections.heading: Scaling Down: Running ICS at a Small Rescue
sections.body:
Most rescues are small. A walker with a broken ankle two kilometres from a road, a child missing from a campsite, a car in a ditch with water rising: these involve six to twenty people, last two to six hours, and will never see a printed Incident Action Plan. The mistake many people make is to conclude that ICS is therefore irrelevant. The opposite is true. The small incident is where the structure is cheapest to apply and where its absence does the most damage per person, because with eight people and no structure, four will duplicate one task and nobody will do two others.

Scaling down means keeping the principles and dropping the paperwork. One person is Command and says so. Assignments are given by objective. Nobody works alone or unsupervised. Everybody is written down on arrival and crossed off on departure. Somebody is watching for hazards. That is the entire irreducible core, and it can be run out of a notebook and one radio channel.

The other half of scaling down is handling untrained help, which at a small rescue is often most of the people present. Bystanders, family members and off-duty passers-by will arrive wanting to assist, and they are a genuine resource and a genuine hazard simultaneously. The workable approach is to accept them, name one person as their supervisor, give them bounded tasks well away from the hazard — carrying, lighting, marking a route, meeting the ambulance at the gate, keeping a path clear — and to be explicit that they may not enter the hazard area. This satisfies their need to help, uses their labour, and keeps them accounted for. Turning them away rarely works; they simply operate outside your view.
steps: Establish and announce command out loud, by name of location: "I'm running this, we'll call it Mill Lane Command." Say it to everyone present, not just to the radio.

Do a scene size-up in under two minutes: what has happened, how many casualties, what hazards exist, what access is available, and what help is needed. Make the call for professional resources now, before anything else, because response time runs in parallel with everything you do next.
Write down every person present, with a time. A page in a notebook is sufficient. This list is what lets you answer 'is everyone out' later, and there is no substitute for it.

State two or three objectives aloud so that everyone hears the same thing. For example: keep the casualty warm and monitored; establish a safe path to the road; get an ambulance to the gate by twenty past.

Appoint a supervisor for each objective and give each supervisor no more than five people. If you have more than about fifteen people, appoint someone to run the tactical work as a whole so you can keep the overview.
Appoint someone whose only job is safety. Give them explicit authority to stop anything, and say so in front of the group so nobody argues with them later.
Set a hazard boundary and control who crosses it. Only people with the right equipment, training and a named supervisor go inside. Everyone else works outside it.
Agree how you will communicate: one radio channel if you have radios, or a named runner if you do not. Confirm that the people furthest away can actually reach you before they walk out of range.
Check in with each supervisor at fixed intervals rather than waiting for them to call you. Every fifteen minutes is a reasonable default; write down what they tell you.
Reassess objectives whenever something material changes: darkness, weather, the casualty's condition, or the arrival of a service that outranks your capability.
Hand over deliberately when professional responders take command. Brief them face to face on situation, objectives, who is where, hazards, and what you have already asked for.

End the incident explicitly. Account for every name on your list, release people formally, remind anyone driving to eat and rest first, and tell the group where to go if they need to talk about it afterwards.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Limits, and Repairing a Broken Incident
sections.body:
ICS fails in a small number of recognisable ways, and knowing their signatures is more useful than memorising any chart.

Freelancing is the classic. An individual or crew, usually well-intentioned and often skilled, self-assigns to a task nobody gave them and tells nobody. The damage is threefold: the task they abandoned goes undone, they may collide with another team's operation, and they are no longer accounted for, so a collapse or a flood surge produces a search for someone whose location is unknown. The cultural fix is stronger than the procedural one — organisations where freelancing is normalised will not be reformed by a form — but the operational fix is check-in, assignment, and periodic contact.

Loss of accountability is the failure that kills rescuers. It looks like a nominal roll that was never updated, people entering a hazard area without passing through a control point, and supervisors who cannot say how many people they have. The repair tools are check-in discipline at a single entry point, an accountability board or T-card rack that is physically maintained, and the personnel accountability report, or PAR: a full poll in which every supervisor confirms by name or number that all their people are present and accounted for. A PAR should be run at fixed intervals during hazardous operations, at any change in strategy, after any sudden event such as a collapse or flash flood, and immediately upon any report of a missing responder. On a small incident it is a headcount against the notebook, and it takes ninety seconds.

Emergency traffic and the mayday are the accountability system's emergency stop. A rescuer in trouble transmits an agreed word — "mayday" is standard in most services — the channel is cleared of all other traffic immediately, and the incident switches to a rescuer-rescue posture. This is a rehearsed procedure in professional services because the ordinary instinct, which is for everyone nearby to converge on the casualty, is exactly wrong and produces multiple casualties. Whoever is in command must resist it, assign a specific team, and keep the rest of the operation intact or shut it down deliberately.

Span-of-control collapse announces itself as a commander whose radio never stops and who has stopped thinking more than sixty seconds ahead. The repair is to appoint an Operations Section Chief and hand over tactical control, which most commanders resist and all of them should do sooner than they do.

The system's honest limits are worth naming. ICS does not supply competence, equipment, or good judgement, and a well-organised incident run by people without the technical skill for the hazard is an orderly disaster rather than a chaotic one. It is also possible to over-apply it: a three-person response does not need a written plan, and imposing ceremony on a small job breeds cynicism that will cost you compliance on the day it matters. Finally, it manages incidents, not organisations — the preparedness, training, mutual-aid agreements and equipment must exist beforehand, because no structure invented at 0200 can conjure a swiftwater team that was never funded.

guides.safetyNote: An organisational chart does not make an unsafe rescue safe. Nobody should enter water, a collapsed structure, a confined space, a swiftwater hydraulic, an avalanche path or a burning building without the training, equipment and backup specific to that hazard, no matter how well the incident is being managed. Confined-space and swiftwater entries in particular kill more would-be rescuers than original victims; roughly 60 percent of confined-space fatalities in industrial datasets are people who went in after someone else. If you are the only trained person present, your first duty is to call for professional response and to stop others from adding themselves to the casualty list.

guides.title: Unified Command in Multi Agency Rescue
guides.summary: How multiple agencies run one rescue: the Incident Command System, when Unified Command is required and who sits at the table, the planning cycle that produces a single Incident Action Plan, communications and accountability, and the failure modes that inquiries keep finding.
guides.safetyNote: This is an organisational reference, not a substitute for accredited incident command training or for the legal framework in your jurisdiction. Command roles carry statutory duties that vary by country and by service; nobody should assume a command position they are not authorised and trained to hold. In any real incident, life safety takes precedence over property and over procedure, and no rescuer should enter a hazard area without check-in, a named supervisor and an accountability system that can confirm they are still there.

sections.heading: Why Command Structure Decides Who Lives
sections.body:
When several organisations respond to the same emergency, the limiting factor on how many people survive
is rarely equipment, courage or even numbers. It is coordination. Two competent agencies working from
different pictures of the same incident will duplicate some tasks, leave others undone, and occasionally
place their own people in danger created by the other. This is not a hypothetical failure mode; it is the
single most consistent finding of major incident inquiries across four decades and several continents.

The clearest illustration remains the World Trade Center attacks of 11 September 2001. The New York Fire
Department and the New York Police Department established separate command posts several blocks apart and
operated on incompatible radio systems. Police helicopters circling the towers observed the north tower
bulging and glowing and transmitted warnings of imminent collapse over police channels. Those
transmissions never reached the firefighters climbing the stairwells, because no mechanism existed to
pass them across. The 9/11 Commission concluded that the lack of unified command and interoperable
communications cost lives that a shared structure might have saved.

The pattern repeats. The Kerslake Report into the Manchester Arena bombing of 22 May 2017 found that
Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service did not arrive at the scene for more than two hours, largely
because commanders acting on fragmentary information declared a marauding-terrorist protocol and held
crews at a rendezvous point that nobody had communicated to the other services. Casualties were carried
out on advertising hoardings by police officers and members of the public. The Grenfell Tower Inquiry's
first-phase report of October 2019 found comparable failures of joint working between the London Fire
Brigade, the Metropolitan Police and the London Ambulance Service, including the absence of any
functioning joint command for a substantial part of the night.

The reason coordination fails is structural rather than personal. Every responding organisation arrives
with its own legal duties, its own doctrine, its own vocabulary, its own radio system and its own
hierarchy that its members trust. Each is internally coherent. Placed side by side without a deliberate
integrating mechanism, they produce parallel operations that touch only by accident. Nobody has to behave
badly for this to happen; it is the default outcome of competent organisations doing their own jobs.

Unified Command is the deliberate mechanism for preventing that default. It is a specific, teachable
structure in which the senior representatives of every agency holding legal authority over some part of an
incident sit together, physically or virtually, and produce one set of objectives and one plan that all
of them execute. It does not merge the agencies, does not remove anyone's statutory responsibility, and
does not require anyone to take orders from another service's chief. Understanding exactly what it does
and does not do is the substance of competent multi-agency response.

sections.heading: Where the Structure Came From
sections.body:
The Incident Command System, of which Unified Command is a component, was not designed in an academic
setting. It was built by working fire officers in southern California in the early 1970s after a
catastrophic season. In September and October 1970 a series of wildfires driven by Santa Ana winds burned
roughly 200 000 hectares across the state in thirteen days, destroying more than 700 structures and
killing sixteen people. The subsequent analysis found that the losses were not principally caused by lack
of resources. Engines and crews arrived in large numbers from many jurisdictions. They could not be
effectively employed because there was no common organisational structure, no shared terminology, no
agreed planning process and no way to integrate agencies that had never worked together.

Congress funded a research programme called FIRESCOPE, an acronym for Firefighting Resources of
California Organized for Potential Emergencies, run jointly by the United States Forest Service and
California fire agencies. Over roughly a decade it produced the ICS, together with the Multi-Agency
Coordination System that sits above it. The design principles were deliberately austere: a common
organisational chart that every agency would adopt, plain terminology instead of agency-specific codes,
modular expansion so the same system serves a two-engine incident and a ten-thousand-person campaign
fire, and a formal planning cycle producing a written plan for each operational period.

Adoption spread from wildfire to structural fire, to hazardous materials, to law enforcement, to
emergency medical services and eventually far beyond emergency response. In the United States the system
was made mandatory by Homeland Security Presidential Directive 5, signed in February 2003, which created
the National Incident Management System. NIMS incorporated ICS essentially unchanged and tied federal
preparedness funding to its adoption, which is why American agencies of every kind now train to it. NIMS
was substantially revised in 2017.

Other countries reached similar conclusions by different routes. The United Kingdom developed the
Gold-Silver-Bronze framework, in which Gold sets strategy, Silver plans tactics and Bronze executes them,
originally in policing after the 1985 Broadwater Farm riot and later generalised. Following the 2005
London bombings and repeated inquiry findings, the UK added the Joint Emergency Services Interoperability
Principles, known as JESIP, published in 2013 and refreshed since, which specify five joint working
principles and a Joint Decision Model. Australia and New Zealand use the Australasian Inter-service
Incident Management System, a close relative of ICS. Canada, much of the Caribbean and many international
humanitarian organisations use ICS derivatives.

The convergence is informative. Independent systems facing the same coordination problem arrived at
similar answers: co-locate the decision-makers, agree objectives before tactics, speak plainly, and write
the plan down. It is worth noting what none of them concluded. No system solved the problem by giving one
service permanent primacy over the others, because in practice the service that should lead changes with
the phase of the incident, and a fixed hierarchy simply relocates the coordination failure rather than
removing it. Every one of these frameworks instead builds a mechanism for negotiating leadership quickly
and explicitly.

sections.heading: The Basic Architecture: Command and the General Staff
sections.body:
Before Unified Command makes sense, the underlying organisation must be clear, because Unified Command
changes only who occupies one box on the chart. Everything below that box works identically.

At the top sits Command, responsible for setting objectives, approving the plan and accepting overall
accountability. Directly supporting Command are three Command Staff positions, each reporting to the
Incident Commander rather than through the operational chain. The Safety Officer monitors hazardous
conditions and, uniquely in the structure, holds delegated authority to stop or alter any operation
judged to present imminent danger without first seeking permission. The Public Information Officer is the
single point for information released to media and the public. The Liaison Officer is the contact point
for assisting and cooperating agencies that are not part of Command itself.

Beneath Command sit the General Staff, four sections whose names are standardised so that a responder
from any agency knows immediately where to go. Operations directs all tactical activity, meaning
everything that is physically done to the incident, and is normally the largest section by far. Planning
collects and evaluates information, tracks the status of every resource, prepares the written Incident
Action Plan and maintains documentation. Logistics provides everything the response needs to function,
including facilities, transport, supplies, food, fuel, communications equipment and medical support for
responders. Finance and Administration tracks costs, handles procurement, processes compensation and
claims, and records time, which matters enormously when reimbursement or litigation follows.

A fifth section, Intelligence and Investigations, may be created for incidents where information gathering
is a major function in its own right, such as terrorism, arson or disease outbreak. It can alternatively
sit within Planning or as a Command Staff position, and the choice depends on how central the function is.

Two structural rules govern how this expands. The first is that only positions actually needed are
activated. On a small incident one person is the Incident Commander and performs all functions personally;
sections are established only when the workload exceeds what Command can manage. The second is span of
control, the number of subordinates any one supervisor directs. ICS doctrine sets an acceptable range of
three to seven, with five as the optimum, and requires the organisation to be subdivided when that range
is exceeded. Operations therefore grows downward through Branches, Divisions, which are geographical, and
Groups, which are functional, then Task Forces and Strike Teams, then single resources.

Every position that is not activated remains the responsibility of the position above it. This is the
rule that makes the system scale continuously rather than in jumps, and it means responsibility is never
accidentally unassigned.

The chart is also deliberately function-based rather than rank-based, which is what allows agencies with
incompatible rank structures to work inside one organisation. A position is filled by whoever is
qualified for it and available, not by whoever holds the most senior badge, and a junior officer holding
a section chief position directs senior officers assigned beneath them for the duration of that
assignment. Services new to the system usually find this the hardest single adjustment to make.

sections.heading: Single Command, Unified Command, and What Triggers the Change
sections.body:
Most incidents run under Single Command: one Incident Commander, drawn from the agency with jurisdiction,
who holds sole authority for objectives and strategy. This is simple, fast and entirely appropriate for a
house fire, a road collision or a lost walker within one authority's boundary. Single Command should be
used whenever it will work, because every additional decision-maker adds delay.

Unified Command is warranted when an incident crosses boundaries in a way that makes any single commander
legally or practically unable to direct the whole response. There are three distinct triggers, and it is
worth separating them because responders often conflate them.

The first is geographic jurisdiction. A wildfire burning across a county line, a river contamination
moving downstream through several districts, or a search spanning national park and private land involves
authorities each of whom has legal power over part of the ground and none over the rest. The second is
functional authority. A structural collapse at a chemical plant may sit entirely within one municipality
yet engage a fire service responsible for rescue, an environmental agency responsible for the release, a
health authority responsible for exposure, a police service responsible for the scene as evidence, and a
workplace safety regulator with statutory powers of its own. No one of them can lawfully direct the
others. The third is level of government. Incidents that draw in local, regional and national bodies
create layered authority that must be reconciled rather than overridden.

The defining feature of Unified Command is that the participating commanders jointly agree a single set
of incident objectives and approve a single Incident Action Plan, while each retains their own agency's
authority, accountability and legal responsibility. They do not vote. They do not take turns. They reach
agreement, and where they cannot, the disagreement is escalated to their parent organisations rather than
resolved by one overruling another on scene.

The single most important operational rule, and the one most often broken, is that Unified Command
designates exactly one Operations Section Chief. That person receives one set of objectives and directs
all tactical resources regardless of which agency supplied them. If two agencies each appoint their own
operations chief and run parallel tactical operations, the structure has failed no matter how cordial the
meetings are. Command by committee at the tactical level is precisely the failure mode Unified Command
exists to prevent.

Selection of the Operations Section Chief follows from the dominant tactical problem at that moment, not
from seniority or from which agency arrived first. On a burning building with people inside, it is a fire
officer. On a hostage situation, it is a police commander. On a mass-casualty triage problem, it may be
an ambulance officer. Because the dominant problem changes, the Operations Section Chief may change
between operational periods, and a mature Unified Command plans that transition deliberately rather than
resisting it.

sections.heading: Who Belongs at the Unified Command Table
sections.body:
One of the commonest practical errors is admitting too many people to Unified Command. A table of fifteen
representatives cannot reach timely agreement, and the structure degenerates into a briefing forum while
tactical decisions drift back to whoever is willing to make them. The doctrine is deliberately
restrictive, and the test has three parts, all of which must be satisfied.

An agency belongs in Unified Command if it has legal jurisdiction or functional authority over some
element of the incident, if it is specifically affected by the incident or by decisions made about it,
and if it is contributing resources of consequence. An agency meeting only one or two of these criteria
is an assisting or cooperating agency and is represented through the Liaison Officer, which gives it a
formal channel without a seat at the decision table.

The representative each agency sends must be able to commit that agency. This is the second common
failure. Sending a knowledgeable but unauthorised officer produces a table where every decision must be
referred elsewhere, which reintroduces exactly the delay Unified Command was built to remove. The
representative needs authority to commit resources, to accept the agreed objectives on their agency's
behalf, and to bind their organisation to the plan. Where the agency's own rules prevent that, the
limitation should be stated openly at the outset so the others can plan around it.

Practical composition varies by incident type. A wildland fire crossing jurisdictions typically seats the
land management agency, the local fire authority and, where structures are threatened, the responsible
municipality. A hazardous materials release seats fire, environmental protection and public health, often
with the facility operator present as a technical specialist rather than a commander. A missing-person
search seats the police, who normally hold primacy, alongside the mountain or cave rescue organisation
providing the specialist capability and any land manager controlling access. A terrorist attack seats
police, fire and ambulance, with police typically holding primacy for the scene overall while fire
retains authority over firefighting and rescue operations and ambulance over clinical priorities.

Private-sector and voluntary organisations require particular care. A utility company, a rail operator, a
pipeline owner or a site occupier often holds indispensable technical knowledge and sometimes statutory
duties. They may belong in Unified Command where their legal responsibility is real, but their commercial
interests are not the same as the public interest, and that tension should be acknowledged rather than
politely ignored.

Finally, Unified Command membership is not permanent. As an incident evolves from rescue through recovery
to investigation and remediation, agencies enter and leave. A formal handover at the start of an
operational period is far safer than a gradual drift in which nobody is certain who is still responsible
for what.

sections.heading: Setting Objectives Everyone Can Execute
sections.body:
The single output that makes Unified Command work is a shared set of incident objectives. Everything else
in the structure exists to produce, communicate and execute them. Objectives state what the response is
trying to achieve during a defined period; they do not state how, because how is the Operations Section's
business.

Good objectives satisfy a small number of demanding criteria. They must be specific enough that a
supervisor can tell whether they have been met. They must be measurable, which usually means attaching a
quantity or a completion state. They must be attainable with the resources realistically available, since
an unattainable objective invites improvisation that nobody has planned for. They must be relevant to the
incident's actual problems rather than to institutional habit. And they must be time-bound to the
operational period, so that progress can be assessed at a fixed point. The standard order of precedence
in rescue is life safety first, incident stabilisation second, property and environmental conservation
third, and every objective set should be readable against that hierarchy.

A weak objective reads: protect the public. A usable one reads: complete evacuation of all residential
properties within 500 metres of the release point by 1400 hours and confirm by door-to-door sweep with
recorded addresses. The second can be assigned, resourced, tracked and reported. The first cannot, and in
a multi-agency setting it will be interpreted differently by each service.

The process by which Unified Command reaches agreement matters as much as the content. The convention is
that each agency representative states, in turn and without interruption, their own agency's priorities,
constraints, legal obligations and limitations. Only after all have spoken does the group construct the
combined set. This sequencing is not politeness; it surfaces conflicts early, when they can be designed
around, rather than mid-shift when they appear as contradictory orders reaching the same crew.

Genuine conflicts do arise and must be named. Police preserving a scene as evidence and fire crews
cutting through it to reach casualties have real, legitimate, opposed interests. Environmental agencies
seeking containment of runoff and firefighters needing water volume are in direct tension. The Unified
Command's job is to decide explicitly, record the decision and its rationale, and communicate it, rather
than to leave the tension to be resolved by whoever happens to be standing at the point of friction.

The agreed objectives are recorded on the ICS Form 202, Incident Objectives, which is signed and becomes
part of the Incident Action Plan. The written record is not bureaucracy. It is what allows a relieving
shift, an arriving resource or a subsequent inquiry to know what was intended and why.

A practical limit on the number of objectives is worth observing. Beyond roughly six to eight for a
single operational period, supervisors stop holding them in mind and begin working to whichever ones
were mentioned most recently. If the incident genuinely presents more than that, it is a signal either
to lengthen the planning horizon by deferring some objectives to a later period, or to divide the
incident and manage the parts separately under an area command.

sections.heading: The Planning Cycle and the Incident Action Plan
sections.body:
Unified Command produces its plan through a formal, repeating cycle usually drawn as a shape called the
Planning P. The vertical stem represents the initial response, which happens once: an
incident is notified, resources respond, an initial commander sizes up the situation and records it on
the ICS Form 201 Incident Briefing, and if Unified Command is warranted the agencies hold their first
joint meeting. The loop at the top then repeats for every operational period.

An operational period is the fixed span of time for which a single plan is written. Twelve hours is the
most common length for sustained incidents, aligning with shift changes; twenty-four hours suits slow
incidents such as flooding, and periods as short as two to four hours may be appropriate in the volatile
early phase of a fast-moving event. The critical discipline is that the period is decided in advance and
the cycle timed backward from the start of the next one, so the plan is ready before the shift it
governs begins.

The written product is the Incident Action Plan. A minimal IAP contains the objectives on Form 202, the
organisation assignment list on Form 203, an assignment list for each division or group on Form 204, the
communications plan on Form 205, the medical plan for responders on Form 206 and a safety message or
analysis on Form 208. In Unified Command every participating commander signs the plan, and that signature is the
formal act by which their agency accepts it.

Two disciplines separate a functioning planning cycle from a paperwork exercise. The Tactics Meeting,
where the Operations Section Chief works out how objectives will be met, must precede the Planning
Meeting where the whole command commits. And Operations, not Planning, writes the tactics.
steps: Confirm the operational period length and the exact start time, and post the planning cycle deadlines where every section chief can see them.
Hold the Unified Command objectives meeting: each agency states its priorities and constraints in turn, then the group agrees the combined objectives and records them on Form 202.
Brief the Command and General Staff on the agreed objectives, so every section is working from the same intent before any tactical planning begins.
Run the Tactics Meeting, led by the Operations Section Chief, using the Form 215 operational planning worksheet to match work assignments against the resources actually available.
Complete the Form 215A safety analysis alongside it, so that each planned assignment carries an identified hazard and a stated mitigation before anyone is committed.
Hold the Planning Meeting, where Operations presents the proposed tactics, Logistics confirms it can supply them, Finance confirms cost authority, and Unified Command approves or amends.
Assemble and reproduce the Incident Action Plan, obtain a signature from every Unified Command member, and distribute it before the operational briefing.
Deliver the operations briefing to supervisors at shift change, confirm understanding by having assignments read back, then execute and assess progress against each objective.

sections.heading: Establishing the Incident Command Post
sections.body:
Co-location is the first of the JESIP principles for a reason: commanders who cannot see and hear each
other do not share a picture of the incident, however good their radios are. The Incident Command Post is
the single physical or virtual location where Unified Command and the supporting staff work, and
establishing it early and well pays for itself many times over.

Siting is a genuine decision, not a matter of where vehicles happened to stop. The post must be outside
any hazard zone with a margin for hazard growth, upwind and uphill of any release, clear of the collapse
zone of damaged structures, which is conventionally at least one and a half times the structure height,
and away from access routes so that arriving and departing traffic does not have to pass through it. It
must have room to grow, because incidents that need Unified Command tend to grow. It should be marked so
it can be found, traditionally by a green light or flag, and its location must be broadcast to every
responding agency, ideally in the first few minutes.

The post's function is decision-making, not spectating. A recurring failure is the accumulation of senior
officers with no assigned role, each seeking a briefing, which consumes the attention of the people who
need to be thinking. Anyone without a position on the organisation chart belongs elsewhere, and the
Liaison Officer exists precisely to absorb them.

Virtual command posts became far more common after 2020 and are workable, but they lose the informal
side-channel that co-location provides, in which one commander overhears another's radio traffic and
recognises a conflict nobody had formally reported. Where a virtual post is unavoidable, the loss should
be compensated by more frequent structured check-ins rather than assumed away.
ingredients: A defensible location outside the hazard zone with vehicle access, marked and communicated to all agencies.
Shelter and lighting adequate for sustained work, whether a command vehicle, a building, or a tent with a generator.
A large-format display surface: maps of the incident area at working scale, plus whiteboards for objectives, the organisation chart and the resource status board.
Radios or gateways covering every agency's operating channels, plus at least one landline or satellite path independent of the local cellular network.
Printed blank ICS forms, particularly 201, 202, 203, 204, 205, 211 and 214, and the means to reproduce a complete Incident Action Plan for distribution.
A dedicated documentation unit member or scribe whose only job is to record decisions, times and the reasoning behind them.
Welfare provision for the command staff themselves: water, food, toilets and a relief plan, because command fatigue degrades judgement faster than physical fatigue degrades work.

sections.heading: Plain Language, Common Terminology and Resource Typing
sections.body:
Multi-agency incidents fail on vocabulary more often than responders expect. Each service develops
shorthand that is efficient internally and opaque across boundaries, and under stress people revert to
what they know. The remedy is a set of unglamorous conventions that must be agreed before the incident,
because nobody negotiates vocabulary at two in the morning.

The first convention is plain language. Numeric radio codes, of which the American ten-code series is the
best known example, mean different things in neighbouring jurisdictions; a code signifying an officer in
distress in one county may mean a routine status change in the next. NIMS requires plain English for all
multi-agency incident communications, and the same principle applies wherever agencies mix. Abbreviations
should be spoken out in full on first use.

The second is common terminology for organisational positions, facilities and resources. When every
agency calls the tactical leader the Operations Section Chief, an arriving crew from three counties away
knows who to find. Facilities are similarly standardised: the Incident Command Post for command, Staging
Areas for resources awaiting assignment, a Base for logistical support, Camps for rest and feeding on
extended incidents, and Helibases and Helispots for aviation.

The third is resource typing, which is more powerful than it appears. A request for two ambulances is
ambiguous, because ambulances differ in crew qualification, carrying capacity and equipment. A typed
request specifies capability against a published standard, so that a Type I resource of a given kind has
defined minimum staffing and equipment. This lets a commander order capability rather than hardware and
know what will arrive. It also permits meaningful mutual aid across borders where the local naming
conventions differ.

The fourth is a standard message format for the initial declaration, which compresses the essential
information into a form that every service can act on. The UK convention is METHANE: Major incident
declared, Exact location, Type of incident, Hazards present and potential, Access routes and directions
of approach, Number and severity of casualties, and Emergency services present and required. Its virtue
is that it is short enough to pass over a poor radio link and complete enough to launch a proportionate
response. Something equivalent should be agreed and drilled wherever METHANE itself is not standard.

The fifth convention is the accountability system, which is a form of terminology in that it defines what
a resource is and where it is. Every responder entering the incident checks in, normally on Form 211, and
is assigned to a supervisor. Nobody self-deploys into the hazard area. Periodic personnel accountability
reports confirm by name that everyone assigned is accounted for, and the practice of calling one after
any significant event, such as a collapse, an evacuation order or a Mayday, is what turns a paper system
into a real one.

sections.heading: Communications and the Interoperability Problem
sections.body:
Interoperability is the ability of different organisations to exchange information when they need to, and
it is a harder problem than buying compatible radios. It has technical, procedural and behavioural layers,
and a failure at any layer defeats investment in the others.

The technical layer is the most visible. Services historically bought equipment on different frequency
bands and later on incompatible digital standards, so that a fire crew and a police unit standing ten
metres apart could not speak. Solutions include shared national networks, of which the British Airwave
system and the American FirstNet are examples, interoperability channels that all agencies programme into
their sets and monitor, and gateway devices that patch two dissimilar systems together at the command
post. Gateways are useful but should be understood as a workaround: they add latency, they usually
require an operator, and they fail silently.

The procedural layer is the ICS Form 205 communications plan, which for each operational period assigns
functions to channels: a command channel for Unified Command and section chiefs, one or more tactical
channels per division or group, a separate channel for air operations, and a dedicated emergency traffic
channel. The plan is distributed as part of the Incident Action Plan, and every supervisor is expected to
know which channel their assignment uses before they are committed.

Radio discipline is the behavioural layer and the one most often neglected. Traffic should be brief,
factual and addressed, using the receiving unit's designator first so that the right person is listening
before the message begins. Instructions with consequences should be read back and confirmed, a practice
borrowed from aviation and now standard in medicine, because comprehension cannot be assumed. Priority
traffic must be able to break through, which means routine traffic stops when emergency traffic is
declared. Under stress, transmission rate rises and clarity falls; commanders who deliberately slow their
own delivery measurably improve the reliability of what is received.

Redundancy deserves explicit planning. Cellular networks fail predictably in disasters, through physical
damage, power loss at cell sites once backup batteries expire after typically four to eight hours, and
congestion as the public and the media saturate capacity. Text messaging often survives when voice calls
do not, because it uses tiny packets that can wait for a gap. Satellite communications, amateur radio
emergency networks and physical runners are all legitimate fallbacks, and the sequence in which they will
be used should be written down rather than improvised.

The final and least technical point is that shared situational awareness, the third JESIP principle, is
not achieved by broadcasting more. It is achieved by structured, scheduled exchanges in which each agency
states what it now knows, what has changed and what it needs, and by the discipline of confirming that
the other party's understanding matches your own rather than assuming it does.

sections.heading: Safety, Risk-Benefit and the Authority to Stop
sections.body:
Rescue is not safe work, and pretending otherwise produces worse decisions than acknowledging it. What
competent command does is make the risk deliberate, proportionate and reviewable, which requires an
explicit framework rather than case-by-case courage.

The framework most widely used in the fire and rescue world is a risk-benefit statement expressed in
three tiers. Responders may accept a high degree of risk, in a calculated and controlled manner, to save
a savable life. They may accept a measured and limited degree of risk to save savable property. They
accept no avoidable risk at all for lives and property already lost. Applying this requires an honest
judgement about savability, and that judgement is the hard part. A person trapped in a collapsed building
who has been unresponsive for forty hours in freezing conditions may still be alive, and the estimate of
probability has to be made rather than avoided.

The Safety Officer is the structural expression of this. In Unified Command the position may be filled by
one agency's officer with assistants from the others, and the assistant safety officers are attached to
the divisions and groups where the hazards are. The defining feature of the role is that it carries
delegated authority to alter, suspend or terminate any operation presenting imminent danger, immediately
and without prior approval from Command. That authority is real and is meant to be used; a Safety Officer
who has never stopped anything is either supervising a very tame incident or not doing the job.

Multi-agency work introduces hazards that no single agency's procedures cover, and these are the ones
that hurt people. A police cordon can trap firefighters. A firefighting water stream can destabilise a
structure that an urban search and rescue team has shored. Helicopter operations can blow debris onto
crews below. A decontamination line placed for one service's needs can force another's casualties through
a contaminated route. The Form 215A safety analysis exists to force these interactions into the open
during planning, by requiring a stated hazard and mitigation against every planned assignment.

Two further disciplines belong here. Fatigue is a hazard that commanders systematically underestimate:
performance after about seventeen hours awake resembles that at a blood alcohol concentration of 0.05
percent, and after twenty-four hours resembles 0.10 percent, which is above the driving limit almost
everywhere. Work-rest ratios and relief planning are safety measures, not comforts. And rehabilitation,
meaning scheduled rotation out of the hazard area for rest, fluids, food and medical monitoring, prevents
the heat illness and cardiac events that kill more responders on many incidents than the incident itself
does.

One further multi-agency hazard is worth naming because it is invisible until it bites: differing risk
thresholds between services. A specialist rescue team and a general response crew may both be competent
and yet hold quite different views of what constitutes acceptable exposure, since their training,
equipment and legal duties differ. Unified Command should surface that difference during objective
setting rather than discovering it when one agency withdraws from a task another has already committed
to.

sections.heading: Information, the Public and the Joint Information Centre
sections.body:
Multi-agency incidents generate an information demand that is itself a hazard if it is not managed.
Contradictory statements from different services destroy public confidence at exactly the moment when
public compliance with evacuation or shelter instructions determines the casualty count. The structure's
answer is to make information a command function with a single owner.

Under Unified Command each participating agency normally retains a Public Information Officer, and these
work together as a Joint Information Centre, sometimes with a lead PIO designated. The principle is one
message, many voices: agencies may each speak, and each may speak about their own operations, but the
facts, the advice to the public and the timeline are agreed before release. Disagreement is resolved
inside the centre, not on camera.

Speed matters more than polish. The evidence from crisis communication research is consistent that the
first credible account of an event tends to anchor public understanding, and that a vacuum is filled
within minutes by speculation and by material from people on scene with telephones. A holding statement
issued quickly, confirming that an incident is occurring, that a response is under way, that information
will follow at a stated time, and giving one specific instruction the public can act on, is more valuable
than a complete statement an hour later. Committing to a next-update time and meeting it builds the
credibility that later instructions depend on.

Accuracy constraints are real and should be stated rather than hidden. Casualty numbers should never be
released before formal confirmation, because early figures are always wrong and correcting them
downward reads as concealment while correcting upward causes panic. Names are released only after next of
kin have been informed. Cause is not speculated on, particularly where a criminal or regulatory
investigation will follow, since a commander's offhand hypothesis can prejudice proceedings for years.

Rumour control is a specific and underrated function. On large incidents a dedicated line or channel for
the public to check claims reduces the load on emergency numbers and gives the response a live indication
of what misinformation is circulating, which is itself planning intelligence.

Two other audiences are easily forgotten. The families of the missing and injured need a dedicated,
staffed channel and a physical reception centre, because they will otherwise appear at the cordon and
must be managed there under the worst possible conditions. And responders themselves need internal
information; crews who learn the state of their own incident from a news broadcast lose trust in their
command quickly, and an internal briefing that precedes each public release is cheap insurance.

Social media has changed the tempo of all of this rather than the principles. Material from the scene now
circulates within seconds, often before the response has arrived, and it is simultaneously a
communication channel, an intelligence source and a vector for false information. Treating it as all
three at once, with someone in the information function actively monitoring rather than only
broadcasting, converts a pressure into an asset.

sections.heading: Above the Incident: Coordination Centres and Area Command
sections.body:
Unified Command manages one incident. Two further layers exist above it, and confusing them with command
is a reliable way to paralyse a response, so the distinction is worth stating precisely: command directs
resources at an incident, coordination supports incidents without directing them.

An Emergency Operations Centre, called by various names in different countries, is a facility where
representatives of many organisations gather to support one or more incidents. Its functions are policy
decisions beyond the incident commander's authority, resource acquisition and allocation across competing
demands, coordination with organisations that are not on scene such as utilities, transport operators and
neighbouring regions, management of the broader consequences of the event including sheltering, welfare
and economic continuity, and information sharing at the strategic level. What an EOC does not do is
direct tactical operations. When an EOC begins telling crews on scene what to do, it has both duplicated
and undermined the incident command structure, and responders receive contradictory instructions.

The relationship should be explicit: the incident commander tells the coordination centre what is needed;
the centre finds it, prioritises it against other demands, and supplies it. Requests flow up, resources
and policy decisions flow down, and tactical direction stays on scene.

Area Command is a different animal and is genuinely a command function. It is established when several
separate incidents are running simultaneously in the same general area, each with its own incident
management team, and someone must set priorities among them and allocate scarce resources between them.
The classic case is a wildfire complex with four fires competing for six helicopters. Where the incidents
are themselves multi-agency, the corresponding structure is Unified Area Command. Area Command sets
objectives and priorities for the incident commanders beneath it but does not manage tactics on any one
incident.

Escalation and de-escalation between these layers should be planned rather than improvised, and the
triggers should be written into pre-existing agreements. Mutual aid arrangements, memoranda of
understanding and standing multi-agency plans made in calm conditions are worth a great deal more than
negotiations conducted during the event. They should settle in advance who can request what, who pays,
what the legal status of a responder operating outside their normal jurisdiction is, whether insurance and
indemnity travel with them, and how the request is authenticated at three in the morning.

The final layer worth naming is political. Ministers, mayors and senior executives will engage with any
significant incident, legitimately, because they carry democratic accountability. Their engagement belongs
at the coordination and policy layer, and a Liaison Officer or a dedicated senior briefer should absorb
it. Allowing political attention to reach the incident command post directly consumes the commander's
scarcest resource, which is uninterrupted thinking time.

sections.heading: Transfer of Command, Demobilisation and the Long Tail
sections.body:
Incidents outlast individuals, and the transitions between commanders are among the most dangerous moments
in a response, because they are precisely when the accumulated understanding of a situation is most likely
to be lost. Transfer of command should therefore be a formal event with a fixed structure, not a
conversation in a car park.

A proper transfer briefing covers the current situation and how it is changing, the objectives in force
and progress against each, the current organisation and who holds which position, the resources assigned
and their status, the safety concerns and any restrictions imposed, the communications plan in force, and
anything the outgoing commander is worried about but cannot evidence. That last item is frequently the
most valuable and is the one most often omitted. The transfer is announced to everyone on the incident,
because a crew acting on instructions from a commander who has left is a real and recurring hazard. In
Unified Command each agency's representative transfers separately, and simultaneous wholesale replacement
of the entire Unified Command should be avoided; staggering the changes preserves continuity.

Demobilisation deserves as much planning as mobilisation and rarely receives it. A written demobilisation
plan, prepared by Planning while the incident is still active, specifies the order in which resources are
released, the checks each must pass before leaving, the routes and rest requirements for travel home, and
the point at which the incident organisation itself is stood down. Releasing resources in the wrong order
strands capability; releasing them without rest kills people on the drive home, which is a leading cause
of responder fatality after large deployments.

The long tail begins as the emergency phase ends. Responsibility usually transfers from the emergency
services to recovery authorities, and this handover is a formal transfer of command in exactly the same
sense, requiring the same briefing discipline. Scene control may pass to investigators, whether police,
a coroner, a workplace safety regulator or an accident investigation body, and evidence preservation
becomes a governing constraint on everything that follows.

Documentation determines what happens over the following years. The unit logs on Form 214, the decision
records, the sequence of Incident Action Plans and the resource records are what an inquiry, a
compensation claim or a criminal prosecution will examine, and they are also what any honest learning
process requires. Contemporaneous records made under pressure are imperfect, and it is far better to
record uncertainty at the time than to reconstruct confidence afterwards. Finally, a structured debrief
should happen while memory is fresh, separated deliberately from any disciplinary process, because a
debrief that people fear will be used against them produces nothing worth having.

Psychological support belongs in the same plan. Exposure to mass casualties, to the deaths of children,
or to the death of a colleague produces predictable effects, and evidence indicates that single-session
compulsory debriefing of the kind popular in the 1990s does not help and may harm. What does help is
sustained access to trained support, monitoring over weeks rather than hours, and a command culture in
which asking for it carries no cost.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and What to Do When Command Breaks Down
sections.body:
Unified Command fails in a small number of recognisable ways, and knowing the signatures allows a
commander to intervene before the failure becomes an outcome. The following are the recurring patterns,
each with the practical correction.

The first is parallel command, where agencies nod at Unified Command in the meeting and then run their
own operations. The signature is two operations chiefs, two staging areas, or crews receiving conflicting
instructions. The correction is to name one Operations Section Chief explicitly, announce it on every
channel, and route all tactical assignment through that person even if the objectives themselves are still
being argued about.

The second is command by committee, where every decision requires consensus among five representatives and
nothing is decided in time to matter. The signature is a lengthening gap between recognising a problem and
acting on it. The correction is to distinguish decisions that genuinely require joint agreement, which is
objectives and strategy, from those that do not, which is nearly everything tactical, and to delegate the
latter downward immediately.

The third is the unfilled Safety Officer position, or a Safety Officer without real authority. The
signature is crews working in the hazard area with no one tracking cumulative exposure and no stop
authority exercised. The correction is immediate appointment, announced with an explicit statement of
delegated authority to halt operations.

The fourth is span of control collapse, where one supervisor has eleven or twenty subordinates. The
signature is a commander who cannot answer where a named crew is. The correction is to insert a layer:
divide the ground geographically into Divisions or functionally into Groups and appoint supervisors, even
if the appointees are less experienced than ideal, because an imperfect supervisor tracking five resources
beats a perfect one tracking twenty.

The fifth is loss of accountability, where responders have entered the hazard area without checking in.
The signature is an inability to state how many people are inside. The correction is to halt further entry,
run a personnel accountability report by name, and re-establish a single controlled entry point before
resuming.

The sixth is fixation, where command continues pursuing an objective that events have overtaken.
Karl Weick's analysis of the Mann Gulch fire of 1949, where thirteen smokejumpers died in Montana partly
because crews would not drop heavy tools that no longer served any purpose, is the standard illustration
of how hard it is to abandon a plan mid-execution. The correction is structural: a scheduled reassessment
at fixed intervals asking explicitly whether the objectives still fit the situation, and a culture in
which any responder can transmit a safety concern without prejudice.

The general principle for recovering a failing incident is to slow down deliberately, re-establish the
minimum viable structure, which is one set of objectives, one operations chief, one accountability system
and one safety officer, and rebuild outward from there rather than attempting to fix everything at once.

guides.title: Signalling for Rescue
guides.summary: SOS, mirror, ground signals, whistle and light.

sections.heading: SOS
sections.body:
The international distress signal is three short, three long, three short — · · · — — — · · · — sent as one unbroken character rather than as the three separate letters S, O and S. That detail is not pedantry. In standard Morse the gap between letters is three time units, and if you insert those gaps you have sent "S O S", which a trained ear hears as three ordinary letters that might mean anything at all. Run together with only the normal one-unit spacing between elements, the nine-element burst has no equivalent anywhere in the alphabet, which is exactly why it was chosen. Telegraphists write it with a bar over the top to mark it as a single prosign rather than a word.

Morse timing is proportional, not absolute, so you may send it fast or slow provided you keep the ratios. One unit is whatever you decide it is; half a second is comfortable for a whistle or a torch. A dot is one unit of sound or light, a dash is three, the gap between elements inside the character is one, and the pause before you repeat the whole thing should be at least seven units — in practice three to five seconds, so the pattern reads as a discrete package instead of a continuous stutter. At half-second units one complete SOS runs about fifteen seconds including the closing pause. Send it, then stop and listen or watch for a full minute before sending again. You cannot hear a reply over your own whistle, and blowing straight through the answer you were waiting for is one of the most common ways a good signal is wasted.

Any medium carries it. A whistle, a torch, a car horn, a mirror flash, a pot struck with a rock, a beam interrupted by your cupped hand, a stone banged against a steel pipe or a scaffolding upright inside a collapsed building — the pattern is the message and the medium only has to be capable of being switched on and off. You need no other Morse to use it. Searchers trained in mountain, water and urban rescue recognise the cadence on sight, and even an untrained observer registers that it is not random by the second repetition.

Beneath SOS sits an older and simpler convention: three of anything, evenly spaced, means distress. Three fires, three gunshots, three whistle blasts, three flashes.
